meta.curriculumNote:
This library contains original mathematics lessons and exercises for the second year of the Moroccan baccalaureate. The topic sequence follows the available pedagogical guidelines for Experimental Sciences and Mathematical Sciences. Dividing the material into short lessons is an instructional choice made by this website.

The references below are copies of Ministry documents hosted on educational websites. These lessons are not an official publication and do not confirm any changes specific to the 2027 examination. For a particular examination session, consult its official reference framework and circulars with your teacher.

The written courses are available in Modern Standard Arabic, French, and English. The seven videos on indeterminate forms contain synthetic Moroccan Darija narration. The visual explanations for the other lessons show written steps without narration, and this distinction is indicated in the player. Existing video frames may contain Darija text. The video count shown for each lesson is the number of files actually available.

lessons.title: Limits and asymptotic behaviour
goals: Determine the domain and one-sided limits.
Choose the appropriate rule and identify indeterminate forms.
Use limits to establish asymptotes.
lessons.intro: A limit answers a question about where a function's values are heading as the variable approaches a number or becomes very large. We distinguish the value at a point from the behaviour nearby. This distinction is essential for understanding continuity and asymptotes.

sections.title: 1. Domain, neighbourhoods, and one-sided limits
sections.body:
Start with the domain \(D_f\). A fraction's denominator must be nonzero, the expression under a square root must be nonnegative, and the argument of \(\ln\) must be strictly positive. Compute a limit only from directions in which the function is defined.

\(x\to a^-\) means approaching from the left, and \(x\to a^+\) means approaching from the right. The limit at \(a\) equals \(\ell\) if both one-sided limits exist and agree, when the domain permits approach from both sides. The value \(f(a)\) need not even be defined.

example.title: One point, two different behaviours
steps: If \(x>0\), the fraction is positive and eventually exceeds every positive number as \(x\to0^+\).
If \(x<0\), the fraction is negative and \(f(x)\to-\infty\) as \(x\to0^-\).
example.answer: \(\lim_{x\to0^+}1/x=+\infty\) and \(\lim_{x\to0^-}1/x=-\infty\). There is no two-sided limit at zero.

sections.title: 2. Operations and signs
sections.body:
If \(f\to\ell\) and \(g\to m\) are finite limits, find the limit of their sum or product by substitution. For a quotient, we require \(m\ne0\). If the denominator tends to zero and the numerator tends to a nonzero number, examine their signs to decide between \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\).

We do not treat \(\infty\) as an ordinary number. Expressions such as \(0/0\), \(\infty/\infty\), and \(\infty-\infty\) require a suitable transformation before drawing a conclusion. To find the limit of a composition, first check its domain and the relevant limit of the outer function.

sections.title: 3. Standard limits and the squeeze theorem
sections.body:
As \(x\to+\infty\), we have \(1/x^p\to0\) for every \(p>0\). As \(x\to0\), \(\sin x/x\to1\), with angles in radians. For logarithms and exponentials, use \(\ln x/x^\alpha\to0\) and \(x^\alpha e^{-x}\to0\) at \(+\infty\), for any \(\alpha>0\).

The squeeze theorem states that if \(u(x)\le f(x)\le v(x)\) near the point and \(u,v\to\ell\), then \(f\to\ell\). For example, \(-|x|\le x\sin(1/x)\le|x|\), so the limit is zero. We do not need a limit for \(\sin(1/x)\), which has none.

sections.title: 4. Polynomials and quotients at infinity
sections.body: For a polynomial, the term of highest degree determines the behaviour at \(\pm\infty\). Factor out the largest power or divide by it. For a quotient \(P/Q\), the limit is zero if the numerator's degree is smaller than the denominator's. If the degrees are equal, the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients. If the numerator's degree is greater, account for the difference in degrees and the sign.

example.title: The limit of a quotient at infinity
steps: Divide the numerator and denominator by \(x^3\), which is nonzero for large \(x\).
\(1/x^2\to0\) and \(4/x^3\to0\), while the denominator tends to one.

sections.title: 5. Asymptotes and relative position
sections.body:
If \(f(x)\to\pm\infty\) as \(x\to a\) from either side, then \(x=a\) is a vertical asymptote. If \(f(x)\to b\) at \(+\infty\) or \(-\infty\), then \(y=b\) is a horizontal asymptote in that direction. The line \(y=ax+b\) is an oblique asymptote if \(f(x)-(ax+b)\to0\).

To determine which graph lies above the other, examine the sign of \(f(x)-(ax+b)\). Finding \(f(x)/x\to a\) alone is insufficient. We also need \(f(x)-ax\to b\). A sketch helps, but the proof comes from the limit and the sign.

summary: Check the domain and signs before substituting.
The two one-sided limits must agree for a two-sided limit to exist.
\(\lim f/g=\ell/m\) if \(m\ne0\).
For \(P/Q\) at infinity, compare the degrees.
Verify an oblique asymptote using \(f(x)-(ax+b)\to0\).
pitfalls: Do not confuse a function's value with its limit.
Division by a quantity approaching zero requires a sign analysis.
Limits involving \(\sin x/x\) require angles in radians.

lessons.title: The seven indeterminate forms
goals: Recognize the seven families.
Understand why a transformation is necessary.
Solve examples without L'Hôpital's rule.
lessons.intro: The same form can lead to different limits. For example, as x approaches zero from the right, x divided by x gives one, x squared divided by x gives zero, and x divided by x squared tends to positive infinity. The form alone does not give the answer.

sections.body:
\[\lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}=4\]

Substitution gives zero divided by zero. Factor \(x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)\), then cancel the common factor for \(x\ne2\). The expression becomes \(x+2\), whose limit is \(4\). The original function remains undefined at \(2\).

\[\lim_{x\to+\infty}\frac{3x^2+2x}{x^2-1}=3\]

Divide the numerator and denominator by \(x^2\) to obtain \(\frac{3+2/x}{1-1/x^2}\to3\). This method is suitable for polynomials. You cannot cancel terms in a sum unless you first rewrite the expression as a product of factors.

\[\lim_{x\to+\infty}(\sqrt{x^2+x}-x)=\frac12\]

Multiply and divide by the conjugate \(\sqrt{x^2+x}+x\). The expression becomes \(\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+x}+x}=\frac1{\sqrt{1+1/x}+1}\to\frac12\). We used \(x>0\). In general, \(\sqrt{x^2}=|x|\).

\[\lim_{x\to0^+}x\ln(1/x)=0\]

Set \(t=1/x\), so \(t\to+\infty\). The expression becomes \(\ln t/t\to0\), a standard limit comparing growth rates. We also deduce \(x\ln x\to0\), although its values are negative near zero on the right.

\[\lim_{x\to+\infty}(1+1/x)^x=e\]

Call the expression \(y>0\). Then \(\ln y=x\ln(1+1/x)\). Setting \(u=1/x\) gives \(\ln y=\ln(1+u)/u\to1\). By continuity of the exponential function, \(y=e^{\ln y}\to e\). This is the result for this example, not a universal value for the form.

\[\lim_{x\to0^+}x^x=1\]

The base is positive. Set \(y=x^x\), giving \(\ln y=x\ln x\to0\). Thus \(y\to e^0=1\). We are computing a limit, not assigning a general definition to \(0^0\).

\[\lim_{x\to+\infty}x^{1/x}=1\]

\(\ln(x^{1/x})=\ln x/x\to0\). Returning to the exponential function gives the limit \(1\). The base must be positive near the direction of approach being studied.

sections.title: Choosing a method for the expression
sections.body: For polynomials, factor or compare degrees. For a difference of square roots, use the conjugate. For trigonometric functions, use standard limits with angles in radians. For a product, rewrite it as a quotient or change variables. For a power \(u^v\) with a positive base, find the limit of \(v\ln u\), then apply the exponential function. Expressions with signs such as \(0\times(-\infty)\) belong to the same family once the sign is accounted for.

summary: An indeterminate form does not determine the result.
Cancel a common factor only when it is nonzero.
Taking logarithms of powers requires a positive base.
A finite limit \(\ln y\to L\) gives \(y\to e^L\).
pitfalls: Do not say that zero divided by zero equals zero or one.
Cancel factors, not terms in a sum.
Do not generalize one example's result to the entire family.

lessons.title: Continuity and the intermediate value theorem
lessons.titleAr: Continuity and the intermediate value theorem
goals: Prove continuity and find a parameter that joins two pieces continuously.
Use the intermediate value theorem to prove existence.
Prove uniqueness and give bounds.
lessons.intro: A function is continuous at a point when its behaviour nearby agrees with its value there. Continuity is more than an unbroken-looking graph. It is a precise condition that we can check by calculation.

sections.title: 1. Continuity at a point and on an interval
sections.body:
For \(f\) to be continuous at \(a\), we require \(a\in D_f\) and \(\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a)\). At a boundary of the domain, take the limit from within the domain. Continuity on an interval means that this condition holds at every point of the interval.

Polynomials are continuous on \(\mathbb R\), and rational functions are continuous on their domains. \(\sqrt{x}\) is continuous on \([0,+\infty[\), and \(\ln x\) on \(]0,+\infty[\). Sums, products, and compositions of continuous functions are continuous wherever the operations are defined. Division requires a nonzero denominator.

sections.title: 2. Piecewise-defined functions
sections.body: Within each piece, use the usual rules. At a joining point, calculate the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit, and the assigned value. All three must agree. If a parameter is unknown, this equality determines its value.

example.title: Finding a parameter for continuity
steps: Continuity requires the value \(a\) to equal this limit.

sections.title: 3. Continuous extension
sections.body: If a function is undefined at \(a\) but has a finite limit \(\ell\), we can add a new point by defining \(\widetilde f(a)=\ell\). This gives a new function that is continuous at \(a\) and agrees with the original function elsewhere. If the limit does not exist or is infinite, no real-valued continuous extension with a finite value is possible.

sections.title: 4. The intermediate value theorem and uniqueness
sections.body: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), every number between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) has at least one preimage in this interval. In particular, if \(f(a)f(b)<0\), there is an \(\alpha\in]a,b[\) such that \(f(\alpha)=0\). To prove uniqueness, also establish that the function is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing, or supply another argument.

example.title: A unique root
example.statement: Prove that \(x^3+x-1=0\) has a unique solution in \(]0,1[\).
steps: \(f(x)=x^3+x-1\) is a polynomial, so it is continuous on \([0,1]\).
\(f(0)=-1\) and \(f(1)=1\), so the intermediate value theorem gives a solution.
\(f^{\prime}(x)=3x^2+1>0\), so the function is strictly increasing and the solution is unique.

sections.title: 5. Bisection and numerical bounds
sections.body:
After proving existence and uniqueness, take the midpoint \(m=(a+b)/2\). If \(f(m)=0\), we have found the root and stop. Otherwise, determine its sign and keep the half-interval across which the sign changes. After \(n\) successive steps, the interval length is \((b-a)/2^n\). If its midpoint is used as an approximation, the error is at most half that length.

In the previous example, \(f(0.68)=-0.005568\) and \(f(0.69)=0.018509\). Therefore \(0.68<\alpha<0.69\). These bounds follow from the signs and strict increase, rather than an unsupported calculator approximation.

summary: Continuity at \(a\) means a finite limit equal to \(f(a)\).
For piecewise functions, compare both one-sided limits with the value.
The intermediate value theorem requires continuity on the closed interval.
Existence and uniqueness each need a justification.
In bisection, the length of the bounding interval halves at every step.
pitfalls: Equal one-sided limits are insufficient if the value at the point is different.
A sign change without continuity does not guarantee a root.
The intermediate value theorem alone does not guarantee a unique root.

lessons.title: Differentiation and tangents
goals: Calculate derivatives and identify their domains.
Write a tangent equation and connect derivatives with increasing and decreasing behaviour.
Distinguish extrema from points of inflection.
lessons.intro: The derivative measures a function's local rate of change and gives the slope of its tangent. Learning the rules is only the beginning. We also need to know when they apply and what they tell us about the graph.

sections.title: 1. The derivative at a point and its meaning
sections.body:
A function is differentiable at \(a\) if the limit \[f^{\prime}(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}h\] exists and is finite. This number is the tangent's slope, and the tangent equation is \[y=f(a)+f^{\prime}(a)(x-a).\]

Differentiability implies continuity. The converse is false. \(|x|\) is continuous at zero, but its left-hand derivative is \(-1\) and its right-hand derivative is \(1\), so it is not differentiable there. An infinite limit of the difference quotient may indicate a vertical half-tangent, not a finite derivative.

sections.title: 2. Standard derivatives
sections.body:
\((x^n)^{\prime}=nx^{n-1}\), \((1/x)^{\prime}=-1/x^2\), and \((\sqrt{x})^{\prime}=1/(2\sqrt{x})\) for \(x>0\). We also have \((\ln x)^{\prime}=1/x\) for \(x>0\), \((e^x)^{\prime}=e^x\), \((\sin x)^{\prime}=\cos x\), and \((\cos x)^{\prime}=-\sin x\).

For rational powers, work on intervals where the function is defined and differentiable. On \(x>0\), the rule \((x^r)^{\prime}=rx^{r-1}\) is valid for every \(r\in\mathbb Q\). Boundary points require a separate study.

sections.title: 3. Sum, product, quotient, and chain rules
sections.body: \[(u+v)^{\prime}=u^{\prime}+v^{\prime},\qquad(uv)^{\prime}=u^{\prime} v+uv^{\prime}.\]\[\left(\frac uv\right)^{\prime}=\frac{u^{\prime} v-uv^{\prime}}{v^2}\quad(v\ne0).\]The chain rule is \((g\circ u)^{\prime}(x)=u^{\prime}(x)g^{\prime}(u(x))\). For example, \((\ln u)^{\prime}=u^{\prime}/u\) if \(u>0\), and \((e^u)^{\prime}=u^{\prime} e^u\). Write down the inner function and its derivative so that you do not forget this factor.

example.title: Combining the chain and product rules
steps: Factor out the common term to make a later sign analysis easier.

sections.title: 4. Monotonicity, extrema, and the second derivative
sections.body:
On an interval, if \(f^{\prime}\ge0\), then \(f\) is nondecreasing. If \(f^{\prime}\le0\), it is nonincreasing. A strictly positive derivative gives strict increase. A derivative that vanishes at some isolated points does not necessarily prevent strict increase.

At an interior point \(a\), a change in the derivative's sign from negative to positive gives a local minimum, and the reverse gives a local maximum. The condition \(f^{\prime}(a)=0\) alone is insufficient. For example, \(x^3\) has no extremum at zero. If \(f^{\prime\prime}>0\), the graph is convex, and if the second derivative is negative, it is concave. An inflection point requires a change in concavity, not merely \(f^{\prime\prime}=0\).

sections.title: 5. Tangents and local approximation
sections.body: Near \(a\), the function can be approximated by \(f(a+h)\approx f(a)+hf^{\prime}(a)\). This is a local approximation, not a general equality. To draw the tangent, we need both the function's value and its derivative at the point. Then check that the line passes through \((a,f(a))\).

example.title: A tangent to a cubic function
example.statement: Find the tangent equation for \(f(x)=x^3-3x\) at \(a=2\).

summary: Differentiability implies continuity.
In the chain rule, remember the derivative of the inner function.
In the quotient rule, the denominator is \(v^2\) and the numerator contains a minus sign.
The tangent equation is \(y=f(a)+f^{\prime}(a)(x-a)\).
The derivative's sign chart determines where the function increases or decreases.
pitfalls: The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives.
A zero derivative does not guarantee an extremum.
Differentiability at a boundary of the domain requires a separate check.

lessons.title: Inverse functions and powers
goals: Prove bijectivity and determine the image of an interval.
Find an inverse while respecting its conditions.
Use the derivative formula for an inverse function.
lessons.intro: An inverse function takes us from an output back to its input. We must ensure that each output has a unique preimage, and determine the domain and image before writing down the inverse.

sections.title: 1. A bijection on an interval
sections.body:
If \(f\) is continuous and strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on an interval \(I\), it is a bijection from \(I\) to \(J=f(I)\). Find the image using the values or limits at the endpoints, taking care to include or exclude endpoints correctly. For each \(y\in J\), there is a unique \(x\in I\) such that \(f(x)=y\).

The inverse function \(f^{-1}:J\to I\) is continuous and has the same direction of monotonicity. The notation \(f^{-1}\) does not mean \(1/f\). In an orthonormal coordinate system, the two graphs are reflections of each other across the line \(y=x\).

sections.title: 2. Finding a formula and its domain
sections.body: To find the inverse, write \(y=f(x)\), solve for \(x\) while respecting the original domain, then rename the new variable if desired. The same expression may give two branches if the domain has not been specified first.

example.title: Inverting a quadratic on a half-line
steps: \(f\) is continuous and strictly increasing on this interval.

sections.title: 3. The derivative of an inverse function
sections.body:
Under the preceding bijection assumptions, let \(a\) be an interior point of \(I\). If \(f\) is differentiable at \(a\) and \(f^{\prime}(a)\ne0\), its inverse is differentiable at \(b=f(a)\), with \[(f^{-1})^{\prime}(b)=\frac1{f^{\prime}(a)}.\]More generally, \((f^{-1})^{\prime}(x)=1/f^{\prime}(f^{-1}(x))\) wherever the conditions hold.

In the previous example, \(a=2\) gives \(b=5\) and \(f^{\prime}(2)=4\), so \((f^{-1})^{\prime}(5)=1/4\). At \(a=0\), the derivative vanishes and the formula cannot be used. Indeed, the inverse \(\sqrt{y-1}\) has a vertical half-tangent at \(1\).

sections.title: 4. nth roots and rational powers
sections.body:
For \(n\in\mathbb{N}^*\), the function \(x\mapsto x^n\) on \([0,+\infty[\) has inverse \(x\mapsto\sqrt[n]x\). If \(n\) is odd, an inverse also exists on all of \(\mathbb R\). For \(x>0\), define \(x^{p/q}=(\sqrt[q]x)^p\) with \(q>0\). The rules \(x^rx^s=x^{r+s}\) and \((x^r)^s=x^{rs}\) hold on this domain.

\((x^r)^{\prime}=rx^{r-1}\) for \(x>0\). At zero and at negative numbers, the domain depends on the precise meaning of the exponent. Do not extend formulas to undefined expressions.

summary: Determine the domain and image before writing the inverse.
Continuity and strict monotonicity guarantee a bijection onto the image.
In general, \(f^{-1}\ne1/f\).
The inverse's derivative is the reciprocal of the original derivative at the preimage, provided that derivative is nonzero.
Working with rational powers on the positive domain avoids ambiguity in their definition.
pitfalls: Do not choose a negative root when the original domain contains only nonnegative values.
Do not substitute the image in place of the preimage in the inverse derivative formula.
If the original derivative is zero, the reciprocal formula cannot be applied directly.

steps: \(f^{\prime}(x)=3x^2+1>0\). The function is continuous with limits \(\pm\infty\), so it is a bijection onto \(\mathbb R\).

steps: The domain is positive, so the differentiation rule applies.

lessons.title: A complete study of a function
lessons.titleAr: A complete study of a function
goals: Carry out a complete study of a rational, logarithmic, or exponential function.
Connect variation tables with asymptotes and the graph.
Use the study to solve an inequality or count solutions.
lessons.intro: A complete study involves more than calculating a derivative. We connect the domain, limits, asymptotes, monotonicity, concavity, and intersections so that the final graph follows from the proof.

sections.title: 1. A work plan that avoids omissions
sections.body:
A practical order is to find the domain, check symmetry if useful, calculate limits at the domain's boundaries, identify asymptotes, find the derivative and its sign, build a variation table, calculate important values and tangents, then draw the graph. If concavity is required, add the second derivative and inflection points. For an equation \(f(x)=m\), use the monotonic branches to count solutions.

Each component of the domain needs a limit at both ends. In the variation table, an excluded value remains a break. Do not draw an arrow passing through a vertical asymptote.

sections.title: 2. Main example, domain and decomposition
sections.body:
Study \[f(x)=\frac{x^2+1}{x-1}.\]The domain is \(\mathbb R\setminus\{1\}\). Polynomial division gives \[f(x)=x+1+\frac2{x-1}.\]This form makes limits, differentiation, and the asymptote easier to find.

At \(1^-\), \(2/(x-1)\to-\infty\), while at \(1^+\) it tends to \(+\infty\). Thus \(x=1\) is a vertical asymptote. At \(\pm\infty\), the difference \(f(x)-(x+1)=2/(x-1)\to0\), so \(y=x+1\) is an oblique asymptote.

sections.title: 3. Derivative, sign, and variation table
sections.body:
\[f^{\prime}(x)=1-\frac2{(x-1)^2}=\frac{(x-1)^2-2}{(x-1)^2}.\]The denominator is positive. The numerator's roots are \(a=1-\sqrt2\) and \(b=1+\sqrt2\). The derivative is positive outside \([a,b]\) and negative inside, with a break at \(1\).

  • Increasing on \(]-\infty,a]\), from \(-\infty\) to \(2-2\sqrt2\).
  • Decreasing on \([a,1[\), down to \(-\infty\).
  • Decreasing on \(]1,b]\), from \(+\infty\) to \(2+2\sqrt2\).
  • Increasing on \([b,+\infty[\), up to \(+\infty\).

Thus \(a\) is the location of a local maximum and \(b\) of a local minimum. Calculate their values using the decomposed expression.

sections.title: 4. Relative position, intersections, and concavity
sections.body:
\(f(x)-(x+1)=2/(x-1)\), so the graph lies below the asymptote when \(x<1\) and above it when \(x>1\). At \(x=0\), \(f(0)=-1\), so the graph passes through \((0,-1)\). It never crosses the horizontal axis because \(x^2+1>0\) always.

The second derivative is \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=4/(x-1)^3\). The graph is concave on \(]-\infty,1[\) and convex on \(]1,+\infty[\). There is no inflection point at \(1\), because that input is outside the domain, even though the sign changes.

The centre of symmetry is \((1,2)\), since \(f(1+h)+f(1-h)=4\) for every \(h\ne0\).

sections.title: 5. A tangent and a justified sketch
sections.body:
At zero, \(f(0)=-1\) and \(f^{\prime}(0)=-1\). The tangent is therefore \(y=-x-1\). On the sketch, mark both asymptotes, the point \((0,-1)\), the extrema, and the directions of change. The two branches do not meet at \(x=1\), and their positions relative to the asymptote must agree with the sign analysis.

An approximate sketch cannot replace calculation. If the graph and table disagree, return to the signs and limits before continuing.

sections.title: 6. Studying a logarithmic function
sections.body:
Take \(g(x)=x-1-\ln x\) on \(]0,+\infty[\). At \(0^+\), the limit is \(+\infty\). At \(+\infty\), write \(g(x)=x(1-1/x-\ln x/x)\to+\infty\). The derivative \(g^{\prime}(x)=(x-1)/x\) is negative before \(1\) and positive after it.

Thus \(g\) has a global minimum at \(1\), with value \(0\). We deduce the important inequality \(\ln x\le x-1\) for every \(x>0\), with equality only at \(x=1\). Studying the function has provided a proof of an inequality.

summary: Write the domain before making any transformation.
Calculate every limit needed for each branch.
The variation table is based on the derivative's sign.
An oblique asymptote requires a difference tending to zero.
The graph brings the results together. It does not replace them.
pitfalls: An excluded input cannot be an inflection point.
A local maximum is not necessarily a maximum over the whole domain.
Dividing by x in a limit at zero requires different reasoning from a limit at infinity.

lessons.title: Sequences and mathematical induction
goals: Prove monotonicity and bounds using induction.
Solve an affine recurrence relation.
Prove convergence, then determine the limit.
lessons.intro: A sequence assigns a number to each natural-number index. We distinguish an explicit formula from a recursive definition, and connect monotonicity and boundedness with the limit. Solving a fixed-point equation alone does not prove convergence.

sections.title: 1. Arithmetic and geometric sequences
sections.body:
If \(u_{n+1}=u_n+r\), the sequence is arithmetic and \(u_n=u_0+nr\). The sum of the \(n+1\) terms from \(u_0\) to \(u_n\) is \((n+1)(u_0+u_n)/2\).

If \(u_{n+1}=qu_n\), then \(u_n=u_0q^n\). If \(q\ne1\), \(\sum_{k=0}^nq^k=(1-q^{n+1})/(1-q)\). If \(|q|<1\), then \(q^n\to0\). If \(q>1\), then \(q^n\to+\infty\). The sequence \(q^n\) alternates without converging when \(q=-1\). When \(q<-1\), its sign alternates while its absolute value grows. For \(u_n=u_0q^n\), this lack of convergence requires \(u_0\ne0\). If \(u_0=0\), every term is zero for any \(q\).

sections.title: 2. Induction, invariant intervals, and monotonicity
sections.body:
A proof by induction needs a base case, an assumption at index \(n\), and a deduction at index \(n+1\). For a sequence \(u_{n+1}=f(u_n)\), proving \(f(I)\subset I\) together with \(u_0\in I\) ensures that all terms remain in \(I\).

Prove monotonicity by studying the sign of \(u_{n+1}-u_n\). The ratio \(u_{n+1}/u_n\) is useful only under appropriate sign and nonzero conditions. An increasing function \(f\) alone does not determine the sequence's monotonicity without considering the initial terms.

sections.title: 3. An affine recurrence
sections.body: For \(u_{n+1}=au_n+b\), if \(a\ne1\), find the fixed point \(\ell=b/(1-a)\), then set \(v_n=u_n-\ell\). We obtain \(v_{n+1}=av_n\), so \[u_n=\ell+(u_0-\ell)a^n.\]If \(|a|<1\), then \(u_n\to\ell\). If \(a=1\), the sequence is arithmetic.

sections.title: 4. Convergence and fixed points
sections.body:
A nondecreasing sequence bounded above converges. A nonincreasing sequence bounded below also converges. After proving convergence, if \(u_{n+1}=f(u_n)\) and \(f\) is continuous at the limit, we can take limits and write \(\ell=f(\ell)\).

The fixed-point equation identifies candidates for the limit, but it does not prove that a limit exists. Use bounds to select the appropriate solution, and induction to show that the sequence remains in a suitable interval.

sections.title: 5. A nonlinear example
sections.body:
Take \(u_0=0\) and \(u_{n+1}=\sqrt{2+u_n}\). By induction, \(0\le u_n\le2\). On \([0,2]\), we have \(\sqrt{2+x}\ge x\), since \(2+x-x^2=(2-x)(x+1)\ge0\). The sequence is therefore nondecreasing and bounded, so it converges.

By continuity, \(\ell=\sqrt{2+\ell}\), or \(\ell^2-\ell-2=0\). The roots are \(2,-1\). Since \(\ell\in[0,2]\), the limit is \(2\).

summary: Check whether indexing begins at zero or one.
Induction requires both a base case and an induction step.
Monotonicity and boundedness can prove convergence.
For \(u_{n+1}=au_n+b\), the fixed point suggests a useful substitution.
Solve the equation for the limit after proving convergence.
pitfalls: Do not replace a sequence by its limit before proving that it converges.
A sum from zero to n contains n plus one terms.
A negative ratio requires care when studying monotonicity.

lessons.title: Logarithmic functions
goals: Determine the domain before any calculation involving ln.
Use logarithm identities and differentiation rules with their conditions.
Solve equations and inequalities, and study a logarithmic function.
lessons.intro: The natural logarithm, written ln, turns products into sums and powers into products. The first question is whether the expression is defined, before deciding which rule to apply. Every argument of ln must be strictly positive. We will connect the domain, identities, derivatives, and limits, then use these tools to find solutions and build variation tables without overlooking the conditions.

sections.title: 1. Domain, sign, and monotonicity
sections.body:
The function \(\ln\) is defined, continuous, and differentiable on \(]0,+\infty[\). We have \(\ln1=0\), \(\ln e=1\), and \((\ln x)^{\prime}=1/x>0\), so it is strictly increasing. Therefore \(\ln x<0\) if \(00\) if \(x>1\).

For \(\ln(u(x))\) to be defined, solve \(u(x)>0\). For example, \(\ln(x^2-4)\) has domain \(]-\infty,-2[\cup]2,+\infty[\). The endpoints minus two and two are excluded because the logarithm of zero is undefined.

sections.title: 2. Identities and logarithms to base a
sections.body:
For \(u>0,v>0,r\in\mathbb R\), we have \[\ln(uv)=\ln u+\ln v,\quad\ln(u/v)=\ln u-\ln v,\quad\ln(u^r)=r\ln u.\] There is no rule stating that \(\ln(u+v)=\ln u+\ln v\). A sum inside a logarithm must be handled according to the expression in the exercise.

If \(a>0,a\ne1\), define \(\log_a x=\ln x/\ln a\) for \(x>0\). Its derivative is \(1/(x\ln a)\). This function is increasing if \(a>1\) and decreasing if \(0

sections.title: 3. Differentiating a composition
sections.body:
If \(u\) is differentiable and positive on an interval, then \[(\ln u(x))^{\prime}=\frac{u^{\prime}(x)}{u(x)}.\] For example, the derivative of \(\ln(2x+1)\) is \(2/(2x+1)\) on \(]-1/2,+\infty[\). Remember the derivative of the inner function in the numerator.

The function \(\ln|x|\) is defined for \(x\ne0\), and its derivative is \(1/x\) on each of the two separate intervals. Thus \(\ln(x^2)=2\ln|x|\) for \(x\ne0\), whereas \(2\ln x\) requires \(x>0\). An identity whose conditions are not satisfied cannot be used to enlarge the domain.

sections.title: 4. Limits and comparisons of growth rates
sections.body:
We know that \[\lim_{x\to0^+}\ln x=-\infty,\qquad\lim_{x\to+\infty}\ln x=+\infty.\] The logarithm grows without bound, but more slowly than every positive power. For every \(\alpha>0\), \[\lim_{x\to+\infty}\frac{\ln x}{x^\alpha}=0,\qquad\lim_{x\to0^+}x^\alpha\ln x=0.\]

Use these standard results only when their conditions hold. We also have \(\lim_{u\to0}\ln(1+u)/u=1\), with \(u>-1\). This follows from the derivative of ln at one. It does not allow us to replace \(\ln(1+u)\) by \(u\) as though they were exactly equal.

sections.title: 5. Equations and inequalities
sections.body:
Strict increase gives \(\ln u=\ln v\iff u=v\) and \(\ln u\le\ln v\iff u\le v\), provided \(u,v>0\). The practical order is to find the domain, transform the expression, solve the resulting relation, then intersect with the domain. Reject every solution outside the domain, even if it came from a correct algebraic calculation.

For example, \(\ln(x-1)\le\ln(4-x)\) has domain \(1

sections.title: 6. Using a function study to prove an inequality
sections.body: To prove an inequality, study the difference between its two sides. If the smallest value of this difference is zero, we obtain the required sign throughout the domain. This method also identifies the equality case and goes beyond merely trying numerical values.

example.title: Proving ln x ≤ x − 1
steps: \(f^{\prime}(x)=1-1/x=(x-1)/x\). The denominator is positive, so the sign is that of \(x-1\).
The function decreases on \(]0,1]\) and increases on \([1,+\infty[\), attaining its smallest value at one.
At \(0^+\), the limit is \(+\infty\). At \(+\infty\), write \(f=x[1-1/x-\ln x/x]\), which also gives the limit \(+\infty\).
example.answer: For every \(x>0\), \(\ln x\le x-1\), with equality only at \(x=1\).

summary: \(D_{\ln u}=\{x:u(x)>0\}\), and ln is strictly increasing on the positive domain.
For \(u,v>0\), \(\ln(uv)=\ln u+\ln v\) and \(\ln(u/v)=\ln u-\ln v\).
\((\ln u)^{\prime}=u^{\prime}/u\) where \(u>0\). Also, \((\ln|x|)^{\prime}=1/x\) for \(x\ne0\).
For every \(\alpha>0\), \(\ln x/x^\alpha\to0\) at \(+\infty\), and \(x^\alpha\ln x\to0\) at \(0^+\).
\(\log_a x=\ln x/\ln a\), with \(a>0,a\ne1,x>0\). The function is decreasing if \(a<1\).
pitfalls: Applying logarithm identities before checking that all arguments are positive.
Confusing \(\ln(u+v)\) with \(\ln u+\ln v\).
Accepting a solution outside the domain, or forgetting \(u^{\prime}\) when differentiating \(\ln u\).

steps: The conditions are \(x>1/2\) and \(x>-2\), so the domain is \(]1/2,+\infty[\).
The inequality is equivalent to \(2x-1\le x+2\), meaning \(x\le3\).
Intersect with the domain. One half is excluded, and three is included because the arguments are positive and equal.

steps: \(g^{\prime}(x)=(1-\ln x)/x^2\). Its sign is positive before \(e\), zero at \(e\), and negative after it.
At \(+\infty\), the limit is zero by comparison of growth rates.
exercises.answer: The global maximum is \(1/e\) at \(x=e\). The limit is \(-\infty\) at \(0^+\) and zero at \(+\infty\).

lessons.title: Exponential functions
goals: Connect exp and ln, and use the laws of powers correctly.
Differentiate exponential functions and solve equations and inequalities.
Compare exponential growth with powers and study a composite function.
lessons.intro: The exponential function exp, also written e to the power x, maps every real number to a strictly positive number. It is the inverse of ln. This relationship allows us to bring a variable out of an exponent when solving equations, and explains why exponentials dominate powers in limits. We must distinguish the exponential with base e from a to the power x, whose direction of change depends on the base.

sections.title: 1. Exp and ln as inverse functions
sections.body:
The function \(x\mapsto e^x\) is defined, continuous, and differentiable on \(\mathbb R\), and all its values belong to \(]0,+\infty[\). We have \(e^0=1\), \(e^1=e\), and \(\ln(e^x)=x\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), while \(e^{\ln t}=t\) requires \(t>0\).

The exponential function never vanishes, a crucial fact when building a sign chart. If a function is written as \(P(x)e^{u(x)}\), its sign is the sign of \(P(x)\) throughout the domain where the complete expression is defined. Approaching zero is different from attaining zero.

sections.title: 2. Calculation rules and base a
sections.body:
For all \(u,v\in\mathbb R\), we have \[e^{u+v}=e^ue^v,\qquad e^{u-v}=\frac{e^u}{e^v},\qquad e^{-u}=\frac1{e^u}.\] The expression \(e^{u+v}\) is not \(e^u+e^v\).

If \(a>0\), define \(a^x=e^{x\ln a}\). For \(a>1\), the function is increasing. For \(0

sections.title: 3. Derivatives, tangents, and convexity
sections.body:
We have \((e^x)^{\prime}=e^x\). If \(u\) is differentiable, then \[(e^{u(x)})^{\prime}=u^{\prime}(x)e^{u(x)}.\] Also, \((a^x)^{\prime}=(\ln a)a^x\) for \(a>0\). For example, the derivative of \(e^{-2x}\) is \(-2e^{-2x}\), not \(e^{-2x}\).

The tangent at zero is \(y=1+x\). To compare it with the graph, study \(h(x)=e^x-1-x\). Its derivative \(e^x-1\) is negative before zero and positive after it, and \(h(0)=0\). Thus \(e^x\ge1+x\) on \(\mathbb R\), with equality only at zero. Also, \((e^x)^{\prime\prime}=e^x>0\), so the graph is convex.

sections.title: 4. Limits to recognize
sections.body:
The basic limits are \[\lim_{x\to+\infty}e^x=+\infty,\qquad\lim_{x\to-\infty}e^x=0.\] For every \(\alpha>0\), as \(x\to+\infty\), use \(x^\alpha/e^x\to0\). For example, \(x^2e^{-x}\to0\), after rewriting it as \(x^2/e^x\).

Near zero, \(\lim_{u\to0}(e^u-1)/u=1\), which follows from the derivative of exp at zero. If the exponent is \(ax\), track the sign of \(a\). At \(+\infty\), the limit of \(e^{ax}\) is \(+\infty\) if \(a>0\), zero if \(a<0\), and one if \(a=0\).

sections.title: 5. Solving while respecting the conditions
sections.body:
Strict increase gives \(e^u=e^v\iff u=v\) and \(e^u\le e^v\iff u\le v\). For \(e^{u(x)}=k\), we need \(k>0\) before writing \(u(x)=\ln k\). If \(k\le0\), there is no real solution.

In an equation containing \(e^{2x}\) and \(e^x\), the substitution \(t=e^x>0\) produces a quadratic equation. Solve for \(t\), keep only positive roots, then return to \(x=\ln t\). If the base satisfies \(0

sections.title: 6. A guided study of a product
sections.body: For a product of a polynomial and an exponential, the product rule is essential. Then factor out the positive exponential term to simplify the sign chart. Limits often require rewriting a negative exponent as a quotient before comparing growth rates. Complete the study with significant points, the function's sign, and its asymptotes.

example.title: Studying f(x) = (x + 1)e⁻ˣ
steps: \(f^{\prime}(x)=e^{-x}-(x+1)e^{-x}=-xe^{-x}\). The exponential factor is positive, so the derivative is positive before zero and negative after it.
The function increases on \(]-\infty,0]\) and decreases on \([0,+\infty[\), with maximum value \(f(0)=1\).
At \(+\infty\), \(f(x)=(x+1)/e^x\to0\). The line \(y=0\) is a horizontal asymptote in this direction.
The only root is \(x=-1\). The function is negative before minus one and positive after it.
example.answer: It rises from \(-\infty\) to \(1\), then falls towards zero from above. Its intersection with the horizontal axis is \((-1,0)\).

summary: \(e^x>0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), and \(\ln(e^x)=x\).
\((e^u)^{\prime}=u^{\prime}e^u\), and \((a^x)^{\prime}=(\ln a)a^x\) for \(a>0\).
\(e^x\to+\infty\) at \(+\infty\), and \(e^x\to0\) at \(-\infty\). For every \(\alpha>0\), \(x^\alpha/e^x\to0\) at \(+\infty\).
\(a^x\) is increasing if \(a>1\), decreasing if \(0<a<1\), and constant if \(a=1\).

lessons.title: Antiderivatives and integration
prerequisites: Standard derivatives and the chain rule
goals: Recognize and verify an antiderivative.
Calculate an integral and an average value.
Choose integration limits and interpret an area.
lessons.intro: Finding an antiderivative reverses differentiation. We ask which function has the given function as its derivative. Integration uses this idea to calculate accumulated quantities and areas. Alongside the calculations, we will interpret signs, choose limits, and check answers by differentiation. The volume application is presented as a geometric extension.

sections.title: 1. Antiderivatives on an interval
sections.body:
On an interval \(I\), \(F\) is an antiderivative of \(f\) if it is differentiable and \(F^{\prime}=f\). Once one is known, all antiderivatives are \(F+C\), where \(C\in\mathbb R\). A condition such as \(F(x_0)=c\) determines the constant. The domain must be an interval for the difference between two antiderivatives to be a single constant.

For \(n\ne-1\), an antiderivative of \(x^n\) is \(x^{n+1}/(n+1)\) on an interval where the powers are valid. The exception \(1/x\) has antiderivative \(\ln|x|\) on an interval not containing zero. Independent constants can be chosen on the two sides of zero. We also have \(e^x\mapsto e^x\), \(\cos x\mapsto\sin x\), and \(\sin x\mapsto-\cos x\).

sections.title: 2. Recognizing a derivative from the chain rule
sections.body:
If \(u\) is differentiable, look for its derivative within the expression. An antiderivative of \(u^{\prime}e^u\) is \(e^u\), and one of \(u^{\prime}/u\) is \(\ln|u|\) if \(u e0\) on the interval. For example, \(2x/(x^2+1)\) has antiderivative \(\ln(x^2+1)\) on \(\mathbb R\).

Also, \(u^{\prime}u^n\mapsto u^{n+1}/(n+1)\) if \(n e-1\), subject to the powers being defined. If \(a e0\), an antiderivative of \(e^{ax+b}\) is \(e^{ax+b}/a\). If \(a=0\), the expression is constant and an antiderivative is \(xe^b\). Add \(C\) to give all solutions, and differentiate to check.

sections.title: 3. Integrals, bounds, and average value
sections.body:
If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(F\) is an antiderivative, then \[\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).\] Also, \(A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\), for \(x\in[a,b]\), satisfies \(A^{\prime}(x)=f(x)\) inside \(]a,b[\). Subtract the value at the lower limit from the value at the upper limit. We have \(\int_a^a f=0\), and reversing the limits reverses the sign. Integration is linear, and additivity over intervals, also called Chasles' relation, allows us to split an integral at an intermediate point.

If \(a\le b\) and \(m\le f(x)\le M\), then \[m(b-a)\le\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\le M(b-a).\] Also, \(f\le g\) gives \(\int_a^b f\le\int_a^b g\). For \(a

sections.title: 4. Integration by parts
sections.body: For functions \(u,v\) of class \(C^1\) on \([a,b]\), use \[\int_a^b uv^{\prime}=[uv]_a^b-\int_a^b u^{\prime}v.\] Choose \(u\) so that differentiation simplifies it, and \(v^{\prime}\) so that its antiderivative is known. Keep the minus sign and evaluate the boundary term at both limits.

example.title: Integrating a product
steps: The first boundary term equals \(e\), and the remaining integral is \(e-1\).
We obtain \(I=e-(e-1)=1\). The result is positive, agreeing with the function's sign.

sections.title: 5. Areas and an application to volumes
sections.body:
In an orthonormal coordinate system, the area between two continuous graphs on \([a,b]\), with \(a\le b\), is \(\mathcal A=\int_a^b|f-g|\). If \(f\ge g\), remove the absolute value and integrate \(f-g\). If the sign changes, split at the intersections. A signed integral can be negative, but an area remains nonnegative.

As an additional application, rotating the region under a continuous function \(f\ge0\) around the horizontal axis gives \(V=\pi\int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx\). Between \(f\ge g\ge0\), the volume is \(\pi\int_a^b(f^2-g^2)\). Square the functions inside the integral, not the result afterwards.

sections.title: 6. Distinguishing integrals from areas
sections.body: Before a geometric calculation, determine which graph is above the other. A rough sketch and a small sign chart prevent many errors. An integral represents signed accumulation. For an area, every part is counted with a nonnegative value.

example.title: A parabola below the axis
example.statement: Calculate \(J=\int_{-1}^{1}(x^2-1)\,dx\), then the area between the graph and the horizontal axis.
steps: An antiderivative is \(F(x)=x^3/3-x\). We have \(F(1)=-2/3\) and \(F(-1)=2/3\).

summary: All antiderivatives on an interval are \(F+C\). An initial condition determines \(C\).
If \(f\) is continuous, \(\int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a)\).
For \(a<b\), the average value is \(\frac1{b-a}\int_a^b f\).
Integration by parts gives \(\int uv^{\prime}=[uv]-\int u^{\prime}v\), with the same limits throughout.
The area between two graphs is \(\int|f-g|\), with the limits in increasing order.
pitfalls: Forgetting the constant in the family of antiderivatives, or applying the power rule to exponent minus one.
Treating a negative integral as a negative area, or forgetting to split the interval where the sign changes.
Changing the minus sign in integration by parts, or subtracting the lower-limit value without parentheses.

exercises.title: An antiderivative with a condition
exercises.statement: On \(]0,+\infty[\), find an antiderivative \(F\) of \(f(x)=2x+3/x\) such that \(F(1)=2\).
exercises.hint: Use linearity, then substitute the condition to find the constant.
steps: All antiderivatives are \(F(x)=x^2+3\ln x+C\). The logarithm is defined because \(x>0\).
Differentiating gives \(F^{\prime}(x)=2x+3/x\), and the condition is satisfied.

exercises.title: Average value
exercises.statement: Calculate the average value of \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([0,2]\), and find \(c\in[0,2]\) such that \(f(c)\) equals this average.

steps: The interval has length two, so \(\mu=(8/3)/2=4/3\).
\(c^2=4/3\) gives \(c=\pm2/\sqrt3\). Only the positive value lies in the interval.

exercises.hint: The exponential is positive. Apply the volume formula to the square of the function.

lessons.title: Differential equations
goals: Solve a first-order equation with constant coefficients.
Use initial conditions.
Recognize the three second-order cases.
lessons.intro: In a differential equation, the unknown is a function connected to its derivatives, rather than a single number. We begin with the basic forms and use initial conditions to select one solution. The general second-order classification covering every discriminant case is presented here as an extension for Mathematical Sciences, to make the level of further study clear.

sections.title: 1. A function as the unknown
sections.body:
A first-order equation requires a function \(y\) differentiable on an interval, and a second-order equation requires a second derivative. Here the coefficients are real constants, and the solutions we write are defined on \(\mathbb R\). Verification means substituting into the equation for every \(x\), not only at the initial point.

A condition such as \(y(x_0)=y_0\) determines the constant in the first-order equations studied here. For second-order equations, we also need \(y^{\prime}(x_0)=v_0\). For these linear equations, the conditions determine a unique solution.

sections.title: 2. The homogeneous equation y′ = ay
sections.body:
If \(a\in\mathbb R\), all solutions of \(y^{\prime}=ay\) are \[y(x)=Ce^{ax},\qquad C\in\mathbb R.\] To see why, differentiate \(ye^{-ax}\). Its derivative is \(e^{-ax}(y^{\prime}-ay)=0\), so this product is constant. This proof retains the zero solution without dividing by \(y\).

With the condition \(y(x_0)=y_0\), we obtain \(y(x)=y_0e^{a(x-x_0)}\). If \(a=0\), the equation is \(y^{\prime}=0\), and the solutions are constant. This case is included in the formula because \(e^0=1\).

sections.title: 3. The affine equation y′ = ay + b
sections.body:
For \(a\ne0\), the constant solution is \(-b/a\). Set \(z=y+b/a\), so that \(z^{\prime}=az\). Therefore \[y=Ce^{ax}-\frac ba.\] With an initial condition, the direct formula is \[y(x)=-\frac ba+\left(y_0+\frac ba\right)e^{a(x-x_0)}.\]

If \(a=0\), do not divide by it. The equation \(y^{\prime}=b\) gives \(y=bx+C\), or \(y=y_0+b(x-x_0)\). If \(a<0\), solutions approach the equilibrium \(-b/a\) at \(+\infty\). If \(a>0\), a nonconstant solution moves away from it.

sections.title: 4. Initial conditions and verification
sections.body: Write the general solution first, then substitute the condition. Next, differentiate the final solution and compare both sides of the equation. This order helps catch an incorrect sign or exponent coefficient before studying monotonicity.

example.title: A solution approaching equilibrium
steps: \(-2y+6=4e^{-2x}=y^{\prime}\), and \(y(0)=1\). The solution increases and approaches \(3\) from below at \(+\infty\).

sections.title: 5. Second order and the three discriminant cases
sections.body:
Extension. In \(y^{\prime\prime}+ay^{\prime}+by=0\), the coefficients \(a,b\) are real constants. Trying \(e^{rx}\) gives the characteristic equation \(r^2+ar+b=0\). Calculate \(\Delta=a^2-4b\).

  • If \(\Delta>0\), the roots \(r_{1,2}=(-a\pm\sqrt\Delta)/2\) are distinct, and the solutions are \(y=Ae^{r_1x}+Be^{r_2x}\).
  • If \(\Delta=0\), the root \(r=-a/2\) is repeated, and the solutions are \(y=(A+Bx)e^{rx}\).
  • If \(\Delta<0\), set \(\alpha=-a/2\) and \(\beta=\sqrt{-\Delta}/2>0\). The solutions are \(y=e^{\alpha x}(A\cos(\beta x)+B\sin(\beta x))\).

In every case, \(A,B\in\mathbb R\). Differentiate the formula and substitute both conditions to solve a system in two unknowns. The factor \(x\) in the repeated-root case is essential.

sections.title: 6. Oscillators and repeated roots
sections.body: For \(\omega>0\), the equation \(y^{\prime\prime}+\omega^2y=0\) has solutions \(A\cos(\omega x)+B\sin(\omega x)\). With conditions at \(x_0\), we obtain \[y=y_0\cos(\omega(x-x_0))+\frac{v_0}{\omega}\sin(\omega(x-x_0)).\] If \(\omega=0\), return to \(y^{\prime\prime}=0\), whose solutions are affine functions, without dividing by zero.

example.title: An example with a repeated root
steps: The first condition gives \(A=1\). The derivative is \(y^{\prime}=(A+B+Bx)e^x\).
For the solution \(y=(1-x)e^x\), we have \(y^{\prime}=-xe^x\) and \(y^{\prime\prime}=-(x+1)e^x\). Substitution makes the left-hand side zero.

summary: \(y^{\prime}=ay\) gives \(y=Ce^{ax}\), including the zero solution.
If \(a\ne0\), the solutions of \(y^{\prime}=ay+b\) are \(Ce^{ax}-b/a\).
If \(a=0\), the solutions of \(y^{\prime}=b\) are \(bx+C\).
For second-order equations, the discriminant's sign determines whether the solution uses two exponentials, a repeated root, or sine and cosine multiplied by an exponential.
Determine the constants from the initial conditions, then check by differentiating and substituting.
pitfalls: Dividing by a zero coefficient, or dividing by the function and losing the zero solution.
Forgetting the factor x in the repeated-root solution.
Using only one condition for a second-order equation, or forgetting exponent and angle coefficients during differentiation.

exercises.title: The case a = 0
exercises.statement: Solve \(y^{\prime}=4\), with \(y(2)=1\).
exercises.hint: The derivative is constant, so the solution is affine.
steps: Check that the derivative of \(4x-7\) is \(4\), and its value at \(2\) is \(1\).

exercises.title: Two distinct real roots
exercises.statement: Solve \(y^{\prime\prime}-3y^{\prime}+2y=0\), with \(y(0)=1\) and \(y^{\prime}(0)=0\).
exercises.hint: Factor the characteristic polynomial, then use both conditions.
steps: \(y^{\prime}=2e^x-2e^{2x}\) and \(y^{\prime\prime}=2e^x-4e^{2x}\). Substitution gives zero, and both conditions hold.

exercises.title: An oscillator
exercises.statement: Solve \(y^{\prime\prime}+4y=0\), with \(y(0)=2\) and \(y^{\prime}(0)=-2\).
exercises.hint: Here \(\omega=2\). Remember the factor two when differentiating.
steps: The values at zero are indeed \(2\) for the function and \(-2\) for its derivative.

quiz.explanation: Two independent constants are needed. The factor x provides the second independent solution in the repeated-root case.

lessons.title: Rolle's theorem, the mean value theorem, and arctangent
lessons.titleAr: Rolle's theorem, the mean value theorem, and arctangent
goals: Check the assumptions of Rolle's theorem and the mean value theorem.
Bound a difference using a derivative.
Study arctan and its compositions.
lessons.intro: These theorems connect a function's behaviour across an interval with its derivative at a point. Correct use starts with the assumptions, before the formula. We will see how Rolle's theorem finds a zero derivative, how the mean value theorem and its inequality bound a change, and how these ideas apply to arctan.

sections.title: 1. Assumptions before conclusions
sections.body:
Throughout this lesson, \(a

Do more than name the theorem. Specify the interval, explain why continuity and differentiability hold, then state the conclusion. For example, \(|x|\) is continuous on \([-1,1]\), but it is not differentiable at zero. That single point prevents Rolle's theorem from being applied on this interval.

sections.title: 2. Rolle's theorem
sections.body:
If the preceding assumptions hold and \(f(a)=f(b)\), there is a \(c\in]a,b[\) such that \(f^{\prime}(c)=0\). Geometrically, there is at least one horizontal tangent. The theorem does not state that \(c\) is unique.

For example, \(f(x)=x^2-3x+2\) on \([1,2]\) is a polynomial, so it is continuous and differentiable. We have \(f(1)=f(2)=0\) and \(f^{\prime}(x)=2x-3\). This gives \(c=3/2\), which does lie in \(]1,2[\). The same method proves the existence of a root of the derivative between two roots of the function.

sections.title: 3. The mean value theorem
sections.body: The mean value theorem replaces the equal-endpoint-values condition with a more general conclusion. There is a \(c\in]a,b[\) with \(f(b)-f(a)=f^{\prime}(c)(b-a)\). The tangent slope at \(c\) equals the slope of the secant through the two endpoints. The theorem guarantees existence even when we cannot calculate \(c\) exactly.

example.title: The point supplied by the mean value theorem
example.statement: Apply the mean value theorem to \(f(x)=\sqrt x\) on \([4,9]\), and determine \(c\).
steps: The square root is continuous on \([4,9]\) and differentiable inside it because every input is positive.

sections.title: 4. The mean value inequality
sections.body:
If \(|f^{\prime}(t)|\leq M\) on an interval, then for any \(x,y\) in that interval, \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq M|x-y|\). This is the mean value inequality. It states that the change in the function cannot exceed \(M\) times the distance between the inputs.

More precisely, if \(m\leq f^{\prime}(t)\leq M\) and \(x0\), the derivative lies between \(1/(1+h)\) and \(1\). Therefore \(h/(1+h)\leq\ln(1+h)\leq h\).

sections.title: 5. Arctan, the inverse of tan
sections.body:
The function tan is a bijection from \(]-\pi/2,\pi/2[\) onto \(\mathbb R\). Its inverse is arctan, defined on \(\mathbb R\), with values in this interval and derivative \((\arctan x)^{\prime}=1/(1+x^2)>0\). We have \(\arctan0=0\), \(\arctan1=\pi/4\), and limits \(\pm\pi/2\) at \(\pm\infty\).

For a composition, \((\arctan u)^{\prime}=u^{\prime}/(1+u^2)\). Respect the original domain of \(u\), even though arctan itself is defined for every real number.

example.title: Proving an identity using a derivative
steps: Set \(g(x)=\arctan x+\arctan(1/x)\), which is defined and differentiable on \(]0,+\infty[\).
Thus \(g\) is constant on this interval. Calculate \(g(1)=2\arctan1=\pi/2\).
example.answer: \(g(x)=\pi/2\) for every \(x>0\). The positivity of \(x\) is essential for choosing the correct constant.

summary: Rolle's theorem requires continuity on \([a,b]\), differentiability on \(]a,b[\), and \(f(a)=f(b)\).
The mean value theorem gives \(f(b)-f(a)=f^{\prime}(c)(b-a)\) at an interior point \(c\).
The mean value inequality uses \(|f^{\prime}|\leq M\) to deduce \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq M|x-y|\).
\(\arctan:\mathbb R\to]-\pi/2,\pi/2[\) is increasing, with derivative \(1/(1+x^2)\).
A derivative that is zero throughout an interval means the function is constant on that interval.
pitfalls: Applying Rolle's theorem using equal endpoint values alone and forgetting differentiability inside the interval.
Assuming that the mean value theorem guarantees a unique point c.
Writing the derivative of arctan(u) without the factor u′, or forgetting the domain of u.

exercises.title: Rolle's theorem with two possible points
exercises.statement: Apply Rolle's theorem to \(f(x)=x^3-3x\) on \([-\sqrt3,\sqrt3]\), and determine all suitable values of \(c\).
exercises.hint: Check the function's endpoint values, then solve f′(c) = 0.
steps: \(f\) is a polynomial, so the continuity and differentiability conditions hold.
Both belong to the open interval \(]-\sqrt3,\sqrt3[\).
exercises.answer: \(c=-1\) and \(c=1\). The theorem does not guarantee uniqueness.

exercises.title: Controlling an approximation
exercises.statement: Use the mean value inequality to show that \(0\leq\sqrt{4{,}04}-2\leq0{,}01\).
exercises.hint: Take \(f(x)=\sqrt x\) on \([4,4{,}04]\), and find an upper bound for its derivative.
steps: The square root is increasing, so \(\sqrt{4{,}04}\geq2\), and the difference is nonnegative.

exercises.title: Studying a composition with arctan
exercises.statement: Let \(h(x)=\arctan(2x)\). Determine its domain, derivative, monotonicity, limits, and tangent equation at zero.
exercises.hint: Use the chain rule, then the values of h and h′ at zero.
steps: \(2x\) is defined for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), as is arctan, so \(D_h=\mathbb R\).
At \(+\infty\), \(2x\to+\infty\), giving the limit \(\pi/2\). At \(-\infty\), the limit is \(-\pi/2\).
exercises.answer: The domain is \(\mathbb R\). The function increases from \(-\pi/2\) towards \(\pi/2\), and its tangent at zero is \(y=2x\).

lessons.title: Adjacent sequences and bounds
goals: Prove that two sequences are adjacent.
Identify a common limit.
Turn bounds into a numerical accuracy guarantee.
lessons.intro: In some problems, a sequence's general term is difficult to calculate. We use two sequences, one increasing and one decreasing, that bound the same number. If the distance between them tends to zero, they have a common limit and provide useful bounds. We can even determine how many steps are needed to achieve a chosen accuracy.

sections.title: 1. Three conditions to check
sections.body:
We call \((u_n)\) and \((v_n)\) adjacent if \((u_n)\) is nondecreasing, \((v_n)\) is nonincreasing, and \(v_n-u_n\to0\). The sequences may stay constant at some stages, so strict monotonicity is not required.

Every condition has a role. A difference tending to zero alone does not guarantee convergence. For \(n\geq1\), \(u_n=n\) and \(v_n=n+1/n\) have this small difference, yet both tend to infinity. Increase and decrease without the vanishing-difference condition can lead to two different limits.

sections.title: 2. Why they converge to the same number
sections.body:
First, we deduce \(u_n\leq v_n\). Indeed, for any \(m\geq n\), \(u_n-v_n\leq u_m-v_m\), and the right-hand side tends to zero. Thus \(u_0\leq u_n\leq v_n\leq v_0\).

The sequence \(u_n\) is nondecreasing and bounded above, while \(v_n\) is nonincreasing and bounded below, so both converge. Let their limits be \(\ell_1,\ell_2\). Since the difference tends to zero, \(\ell_2-\ell_1=0\). This gives useful bounds for every \(n\), namely \(u_n\leq\ell\leq v_n\).

sections.title: 3. A recurrence bringing the bounds closer
sections.body: For coupled sequences, start by calculating the new difference \(d_{n+1}=v_{n+1}-u_{n+1}\). If \(d_{n+1}=q d_n\) with \(0

example.title: A geometric difference and a constant sum
steps: The difference tends to zero, so the sequences are adjacent and have a common limit \(\ell\).
From the sum and difference, we deduce \(u_n=2-3^{-n}\) and \(v_n=2+3^{-n}\).

sections.title: 4. Bisection as a pair of adjacent sequences
sections.body: To approximate the unique solution of \(f(x)=0\) on an interval, use continuity and a sign change. Each step retains the solution in one half of the interval. The left endpoints increase, the right endpoints decrease, and the length halves. Keep the justification for the solution's existence explicit.

example.title: Bounding a square root
example.statement: Construct two sequences converging to \(\sqrt2\), starting from \([1,2]\).
steps: Set \(u_0=1\) and \(v_0=2\). Squaring is increasing on positive numbers, and \(1^2<2<2^2\).
If \(m_n^2>2\), set \(u_{n+1}=u_n\) and \(v_{n+1}=m_n\). If equality occurs, stop or set both bounds equal to the solution.
We always have \(u_n\leq\sqrt2\leq v_n\), with \(u_n\) nondecreasing and \(v_n\) nonincreasing.
Before stopping, \(v_n-u_n=2^{-n}\to0\), so the common limit is \(\sqrt2\).
example.answer: The first two bounding intervals after the initial one are \([1,3/2]\), then \([5/4,3/2]\).

sections.title: 5. From a theoretical result to numerical accuracy
sections.body:
From \(u_n\leq\ell\leq v_n\), we obtain \(|\ell-u_n|\leq v_n-u_n\). If we choose the midpoint \(m_n=(u_n+v_n)/2\), the error is at most half the length, so \(|m_n-\ell|\leq(v_n-u_n)/2\).

To achieve an accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\), solve an inequality for \(n\). In bisection starting from an interval of length one, the midpoint approximation has error at most \(2^{-n-1}\). Displayed decimal digits alone do not prove accuracy. The guarantee must follow from established bounds.

summary: Adjacency requires the first sequence to be nondecreasing, the second to be nonincreasing, and their difference to tend to zero.
Both sequences converge to the same \(\ell\), with \(u_n\leq\ell\leq v_n\) at every index.
For coupled sequences, \(d_n=v_n-u_n\) often simplifies the calculation.
An invariant quantity, such as a weighted sum, helps identify the common limit.
The midpoint guarantees an error no greater than half the bounding interval's width.
pitfalls: Proving that the difference tends to zero and announcing convergence without monotonicity or bounds.
Replacing the wrong endpoint during bisection and losing the solution from the interval.
Assuming the limit is the initial midpoint without proving that this midpoint remains fixed.

exercises.title: Two explicit formulas
exercises.statement: For \(n\geq0\), let \(u_n=2-1/(n+1)\) and \(v_n=2+2/(n+1)\). Prove adjacency and find the smallest index for which the bounding interval's width is at most \(0{,}01\).
exercises.hint: Compare the reciprocal of n + 1 with that of n + 2, then calculate the difference.
steps: \(1/(n+1)\) is decreasing, so \(u_n\) is increasing and \(v_n\) is decreasing.
\(v_n-u_n=3/(n+1)\to0\), so the sequences are adjacent. Their explicit formulas give the common limit \(2\).
exercises.answer: The common limit is \(2\), and the smallest required index is \(299\).

exercises.title: A weighted invariant
exercises.statement: Let \(u_0=0\), \(v_0=6\), \(u_{n+1}=(u_n+v_n)/2\), and \(v_{n+1}=(u_n+3v_n)/4\). Prove adjacency and find the limit.
exercises.hint: Calculate \(d_{n+1}\), then try the quantity \(u_n+2v_n\).
steps: \(u_{n+1}-u_n=d_n/2>0\), and \(v_{n+1}-v_n=-d_n/4<0\). Thus the sequences are adjacent.
\(u_{n+1}+2v_{n+1}=u_n+2v_n\), and this quantity equals \(12\) from the initial values.
Calling the common limit \(\ell\), we have \(3\ell=12\), so \(\ell=4\).
exercises.answer: The common limit is \(4\). This can also be checked from \(u_n=4-4/4^n\) and \(v_n=4+2/4^n\).

exercises.title: Four bisection steps
exercises.statement: Approximate \(\sqrt3\) by bisection starting from \([1,2]\). Give the bounds after four steps and the guaranteed error of the midpoint approximation.
exercises.hint: At each step, compare the square of the midpoint with three.
steps: The midpoint is \(3/2\), and its square is \(9/4<3\), giving \([3/2,2]\).
The midpoint is \(7/4\), and its square is \(49/16>3\), giving \([3/2,7/4]\).
The midpoint is \(13/8\), and its square is \(169/64<3\), giving \([13/8,7/4]\).
The midpoint is \(27/16\), and its square is \(729/256<3\), giving \([27/16,7/4]\).
The interval's width is \(1/16\), and its midpoint is \(55/32\), so the midpoint error is at most \(1/32\).

choices: No, the appropriate monotonicity is also needed
Yes, if the terms are positive
quiz.explanation: For example, for n ≥ 1, the sequences n and n + 1/n both tend to infinity even though their difference tends to zero.

quiz.explanation: The farthest point of the interval from its midpoint is half the interval's length away.

lessons.title: Integration, integral functions, and Riemann sums
lessons.titleAr: Integration, integral functions, and Riemann sums
goals: Make a substitution and transform the integration limits.
Differentiate a function defined by an integral.
Recognize and calculate the limit of a Riemann sum.
lessons.intro: This lesson connects integration with three ideas. Substitution simplifies some calculations, the fundamental theorem allows us to differentiate a function defined by an integral without an explicit antiderivative, and Riemann sums turn a large sum's limit into a definite integral. Each technique has features to look for before beginning.

sections.title: 1. Recognizing a useful substitution
sections.body:
If \(\varphi\) is of class \(C^1\) on \([a,b]\) and \(f\) is continuous on an interval containing the image of that interval, then \[\int_a^b f(\varphi(x))\varphi^{\prime}(x)\,dx=\int_{\varphi(a)}^{\varphi(b)}f(t)\,dt.\] Look for an inner function whose derivative also appears in the expression, possibly up to a constant factor.

The notation \(dt=\varphi^{\prime}(x)dx\) organizes the substitution. The new limits must correspond to the new variable, and no unexplained \(x\) should remain in the final integral.

example.title: A substitution leading to a logarithm
steps: The denominator \(1+x^2\) is positive on \([0,1]\), so the integrand is continuous and the integral is defined.

sections.title: 2. Limits and orientation
sections.body:
The new variable may decrease as the original variable increases. Do not reorder the limits without tracking the sign. For example, \(t=1-x\) gives \(dt=-dx\), and \(x:0\to1\) corresponds to \(t:1\to0\). Thus \(\int_0^1 e^{1-x}dx=-\int_1^0 e^tdt=\int_0^1e^tdt=e-1\).

If you find an antiderivative in the new variable and return to \(x\), use the original limits. If you keep \(t\), use the transformed limits. Mixing these choices changes the answer.

sections.title: 3. A function defined by an integral
sections.body:
If \(f\) is continuous on an interval \(I\) and \(a\in I\), the function \(F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)dt\) is differentiable in the interior of \(I\), with \(F^{\prime}(x)=f(x)\) there. At an endpoint included in the domain, use the appropriate one-sided derivative. The variable \(t\) inside the integral is a dummy variable, while \(x\) is the function's variable.

An antiderivative in familiar closed form is not needed to study \(F\). For example, \(F(x)=\int_0^x e^{-t^2}dt\) is defined on \(\mathbb R\), and \(F^{\prime}(x)=e^{-x^2}>0\), so it is strictly increasing. We also have \(F(0)=0\) immediately.

sections.title: 4. Two limits depending on x
sections.body: If \(u,v\) are differentiable and \(f\) is continuous on a suitable interval, additivity of integrals gives \(G(x)=F(v(x))-F(u(x))\). The chain rule then gives \[G^{\prime}(x)=v^{\prime}(x)f(v(x))-u^{\prime}(x)f(u(x)).\] The minus sign comes from the lower limit.

example.title: Differentiating without finding an antiderivative
steps: The function \(t\mapsto1/(1+t^2)\) is continuous on \(\mathbb R\), and the limits \(x,x^2\) are differentiable. Thus \(G\) is defined and differentiable on \(\mathbb R\).
The upper limit \(v(x)=x^2\) has derivative \(2x\), giving \(2x/(1+x^4)\).
The lower limit \(u(x)=x\) has derivative \(1\), and we subtract \(1/(1+x^2)\).
example.answer: \(G^{\prime}(x)=\dfrac{2x}{1+x^4}-\dfrac1{1+x^2}\). This remains valid when \(x^2<x\), because the integral is oriented.

sections.title: 5. Identifying a Riemann sum
sections.body:
For \(f\) continuous on \([a,b]\), divide the interval into \(n\) parts of width \(\Delta x=(b-a)/n\). Then \[\Delta x\sum_{k=1}^n f(a+k\Delta x)\longrightarrow\int_a^b f(x)dx.\] Identify the width, the sample point, and the function.

For example, \(n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n(k/n)^2\) is a Riemann sum for \(x^2\) on \([0,1]\). Its limit is \(\int_0^1x^2dx=1/3\). Having \(n\) terms alone is insufficient. The factor representing the width is also needed.

sections.title: 6. Choosing the right interpretation
sections.body:
In each exercise, ask whether the task is to evaluate an integral, differentiate a function, or find a sum's limit. For differentiation, avoid spending time searching for an antiderivative. For a Riemann sum, factor out the appropriate power of \(n\) so that \(1/n\) and a function of \(k/n\) appear.

Check domains before calculating. A logarithm requires a positive argument, and a square root requires a nonnegative argument. For substitution, continuity over the whole interval ensures that the expression does not pass through an excluded point.

summary: In substitution, transform the expression, differential, and limits together.
\(\big(\int_a^x f(t)dt\big)^{\prime}=f(x)\) if \(f\) is continuous.
\(\big(\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)}f(t)dt\big)^{\prime}=v^{\prime} f(v)-u^{\prime} f(u)\).
On \([0,1]\), \(\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^nf(k/n)\to\int_0^1f(x)dx\).
Before applying a technique, check continuity and the expression's domain.
pitfalls: Changing variables while keeping the old limits without returning to the original variable.
Forgetting the derivative of a variable limit or the minus sign from the lower limit.
Treating a sum as a Riemann sum without the width factor, often 1/n.

exercises.title: A substitution involving a square root
exercises.statement: Calculate \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^1 3x^2\sqrt{1+x^3}\,dx\).
exercises.hint: Take \(t=1+x^3\). Its derivative appears in front of the square root.
steps: \(1+x^3\geq1\) on \([0,1]\), so the expression is continuous.

exercises.title: A logarithmic integration limit
exercises.statement: Let \(H(x)=\displaystyle\int_1^{\ln x}e^{t^2}dt\). Determine its domain, derivative, and monotonicity, and solve \(H(x)=0\).
exercises.hint: The integrand is continuous on R. The only restriction comes from ln x.
steps: The chain rule gives \(H^{\prime}(x)=e^{(\ln x)^2}/x>0\). Thus \(H\) is strictly increasing.
\(H(e)=\int_1^1e^{t^2}dt=0\). Since the function is strictly increasing, this root is unique.
exercises.answer: The domain is \(]0,+\infty[\), the derivative is \(e^{(\ln x)^2}/x\), and the only solution is \(x=e\).

exercises.title: Recognizing an integral within a sum
exercises.statement: Find the limit of \(S_n=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{n}{n^2+k^2}\).
exercises.hint: Divide the numerator and denominator by \(n^2\) to reveal \(1/n\).
steps: By the Riemann sum theorem, the limit is \(\int_0^1dx/(1+x^2)\).

lessons.title: Complex numbers
goals: Calculate in algebraic form and use the complex conjugate.
Connect modulus and argument with trigonometric form.
Solve a quadratic equation with real coefficients.
lessons.intro: In \(\mathbb R\), the equation \(x^2+1=0\) has no solution. In \(\mathbb C\), we use the number \(i\), which satisfies \(i^2=-1\). This extends our calculations while keeping them organized. Algebraic form helps with addition, while trigonometric form helps with products and powers.

sections.title: 1. Algebraic form and equality
sections.body:
Every complex number has a unique expression \(z=a+ib\), where \(a,b\in\mathbb R\). We call \(a=\operatorname{Re}(z)\) the real part and \(b=\operatorname{Im}(z)\) the imaginary part. The imaginary part is \(b\), not \(ib\).

For \(a+ib=c+id\), we need \(a=c\) and \(b=d\). In addition, collect like parts. In multiplication, expand, then replace \(i^2\) by \(-1\).

The powers of \(i\) repeat every four steps, with \(i^0=1\), \(i^1=i\), \(i^2=-1\), \(i^3=-i\), and \(i^4=1\). To calculate a large power, find the remainder when the exponent is divided by four. Real numbers are included among complex numbers. They are exactly those with zero imaginary part.

sections.title: 2. Conjugation and division
sections.body:
The conjugate of \(z=a+ib\) is \(\overline z=a-ib\). We have \(z\overline z=a^2+b^2\), a positive real number if \(z\ne0\). To divide by a nonzero complex number, multiply the numerator and denominator by the denominator's conjugate.

The identities \(\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w\) and \(\overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w\) are also useful. This operation changes the form of the fraction without changing its value.

example.title: A real denominator
steps: Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(1+i\).
The numerator is \((3+2i)(1+i)=1+5i\), and the denominator is \((1-i)(1+i)=2\).

sections.title: 3. Modulus and argument
sections.body:
The modulus is \(|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\). It represents the distance from the origin to the point with complex coordinate \(z\). A nonzero complex number has an argument \(\theta\), defined modulo \(2\pi\), and can be written \(z=|z|(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\).

Use \(\cos\theta=a/|z|\) and \(\sin\theta=b/|z|\), and identify the correct quadrant. Zero has no argument. Do not use \(\arctan(b/a)\) without determining the quadrant, because the same ratio may describe two opposite directions. Arguments have multiple valid values differing by \(2k\pi\), where \(k\) is an integer, and all describe the same direction. For example, \(1+i\) has modulus \(\sqrt2\) and a suitable argument \(\pi/4\).

sections.title: 4. Euler's notation and de Moivre's formula
sections.body:
The notation \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\) abbreviates trigonometric form. If \(z=re^{i\theta}\) and \(w=se^{i\varphi}\), then \(zw=rs e^{i(\theta+\varphi)}\). For division, provided \(w\ne0\), divide the moduli and subtract the arguments.

For a natural number \(n\), de Moivre's formula is \((re^{i\theta})^n=r^ne^{in\theta}\). The modulus must also be raised to the power. It is not enough to multiply only the argument by \(n\).

example.title: A power without a lengthy expansion

sections.title: 5. Quadratic equations
sections.body:
For \(az^2+bz+c=0\) with real coefficients and \(a\ne0\), calculate \(\Delta=b^2-4ac\). A positive discriminant gives two real solutions, and zero gives a repeated root. If it is negative,

\[z_1=\frac{-b+i\sqrt{-\Delta}}{2a},\qquad z_2=\frac{-b-i\sqrt{-\Delta}}{2a}.\]

The two solutions are conjugates. Check the calculation using \(z_1+z_2=-b/a\) and \(z_1z_2=c/a\). For example, \(z^2-4z+13=0\) has \(\Delta=-36\), with solutions \(2+3i\) and \(2-3i\).

summary: \(i^2=-1\), and \(a+ib=c+id\) requires \(a=c\) and \(b=d\).
\(\overline{a+ib}=a-ib\), and \(z\overline z=|z|^2\).
For \(z\ne0\), \(z=re^{i\theta}\) and \(z^n=r^ne^{in\theta}\). Arguments are understood modulo \(2\pi\).
If \(\Delta<0\), the solutions are \((-b\pm i\sqrt{-\Delta})/(2a)\).
pitfalls: Do not replace \(i^2\) by \(1\). It equals \(-1\).
Division requires a nonzero denominator, and an argument requires a nonzero complex number.
The modulus of a sum is not always the sum of the moduli. An argument must use the correct quadrant.

exercises.statement: Let \(z_1=2-i\) and \(z_2=1+2i\). Calculate \(z_1z_2\) and \(z_1/z_2\).
exercises.hint: For division, multiply by the denominator's conjugate.

exercises.title: Trigonometric form and a power
exercises.statement: Let \(z=-1+i\sqrt3\). Determine its modulus and an argument, then calculate \(z^3\).
exercises.hint: The point lies in the second quadrant.

exercises.title: Solving an equation and checking the result
exercises.statement: In \(\mathbb C\), solve \(z^2+2z+5=0\), and check the sum and product of the solutions.
exercises.hint: The discriminant is negative, so the solutions are not real.
steps: The sum is \(-2\), and the product is \((-1+2i)(-1-2i)=1+4=5\).

lessons.title: Complex numbers, advanced Mathematical Sciences
goals: Solve an equation with complex coefficients.
Determine all nth roots.
Identify a transformation from its complex expression.
lessons.intro: In Mathematical Sciences, complex numbers provide further tools for equations and geometry. Here the coefficients can themselves be complex, and finding roots requires an organized use of modulus and argument. We will connect solutions with points in the plane and see how a short expression determines an entire transformation.

sections.title: 1. A quadratic equation in ℂ
sections.body:
The equation \(Az^2+Bz+C=0\), with \(A\ne0\) and \(A,B,C\in\mathbb C\), is solved using \(\Delta=B^2-4AC\). Choose \(\delta\) such that \(\delta^2=\Delta\), then \(z=(-B\pm\delta)/(2A)\). If \(\Delta=0\), there is a repeated root.

In \(\mathbb C\), do not separate cases by the sign of \(\Delta\), because the ordering into positive and negative does not apply to a general complex number. The roots are also not necessarily conjugates when the coefficients are nonreal.

example.title: An equation with nonreal coefficients
steps: Check the sum \(z_1+z_2=2+i\) and product \(z_1z_2=1+i\), as required by the equation's coefficients.

sections.title: 2. Finding a complex square root
sections.body:
To solve \((u+iv)^2=a+ib\), equate real and imaginary parts to get \(u^2-v^2=a\) and \(2uv=b\). We also have \(u^2+v^2=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\), from the modulus relation.

Add and subtract to obtain \(u^2=(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}+a)/2\) and \(v^2=(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a)/2\). The signs are not independent. They must satisfy \(2uv=b\). For a square root of \(3+4i\), for example, we get \(u^2=4\), \(v^2=1\), and \(uv=2\). The roots are therefore \(2+i\) and \(-2-i\).

sections.title: 3. All nth roots
sections.body:
If \(w=\rho e^{i\theta}\ne0\) and \(n\in\mathbb N^*\), the solutions of \(z^n=w\) are \[z_k=\rho^{1/n}e^{i(\theta+2k\pi)/n},\quad k=0,\ldots,n-1.\] Divide the argument by \(n\), while retaining all the angles arising from \(2k\pi\). The solutions are distinct and equally spaced around a circle.

The roots of unity follow by choosing \(\rho=1\) and \(\theta=0\). If \(w=0\), the only solution is \(z=0\), so there are not \(n\) distinct solutions.

example.title: The three cube roots of 8i
example.statement: Solve \(z^3=8i\), and give the solutions in algebraic form.
example.answer: \(\{\sqrt3+i,-\sqrt3+i,-2i\}\). The corresponding points form an equilateral triangle on a circle centred at the origin with radius \(2\).

sections.title: 4. Interpreting a complex affine transformation
sections.body:
For \(z^{\prime}=az+b\), with \(a e0\), if \(a=1\), we have a translation by the vector with complex coordinate \(b\). If \(a e1\), the fixed point has coordinate \(\omega=b/(1-a)\), and we write \(z^{\prime}-\omega=a(z-\omega)\).

If \(a\) is a nonzero real number, the transformation is a homothety with ratio \(a\). If \(|a|=1\) and \(a e1\), it is a rotation through angle \(\arg a\). In general, it is a direct similarity with scale factor \(|a|\) and angle \(\arg a\). For example, \(z^{\prime}=iz+1-i\) is a rotation with centre at complex coordinate \(1\) and angle \(\pi/2\).

Find a composition by substitution. If \(f(z)=az+b\) and \(g(z)=cz+d\), then \(g(f(z))=caz+cb+d\). The order matters because the constant term can change.

sections.title: 5. Translating a calculation into geometry
sections.body:
The distance \(AB\) is \(|z_B-z_A|\). For three distinct points, the argument of \((z_C-z_A)/(z_B-z_A)\) is the directed angle from \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) to \(\overrightarrow{AC}\), modulo \(2\pi\). A real quotient means the points are collinear, and a purely imaginary quotient means the directions are perpendicular.

The equation \(|z-a|=r\), with \(r>0\), describes a circle. The equality \(|z-a|=|z-b|\), with \(a\ne b\), describes the perpendicular bisector of the segment. Always exclude zero denominators before division, then state the geometric conclusion clearly.

summary: For \(Az^2+Bz+C=0\), calculate \(\Delta\), find \(\delta^2=\Delta\), then apply the formula.
For a root \(u+iv\), the condition \(2uv=b\) determines the signs.
If \(w\ne0\), it has \(n\) distinct nth roots, whose successive arguments differ by \(2\pi/n\).
\(z^{\prime}=az+b\), with \(a\ne1\), has fixed centre \(b/(1-a)\).
Modulus measures distance, and the argument of a quotient gives a directed angle.
pitfalls: Using the sign of a discriminant as in the real case when the coefficients are complex.
Giving only one root of zⁿ = w and forgetting the other values of k.
Finding a transformation's centre by solving az + b = 0 instead of the fixed-point equation az + b = z.

exercises.title: A quadratic with an imaginary coefficient
exercises.statement: Solve \(z^2-2iz-2=0\), and check the product of the roots.
exercises.hint: Remember that \((-2i)^2=-4\).
steps: The product is \((1+i)(-1+i)=-1+i-i+i^2=-2\), equal to the constant term because the leading coefficient is one.

exercises.title: Four roots on a circle
exercises.statement: Solve \(z^4=-16\), then describe the geometric figure formed by the solution points.
steps: The arguments increase by \(\pi/2\), and all moduli equal \(2\), so the points are the vertices of a square centred at the origin.
exercises.answer: The four solutions are \(\pm\sqrt2\pm i\sqrt2\), with all combinations of the two signs. They form a square on a circle of radius \(2\).

exercises.title: Identifying a homothety
exercises.statement: Study \(T:z\mapsto-2z+3+i\). Determine its type, centre, and ratio, then find the image of the point with complex coordinate \(1+i\).
exercises.hint: Solve the fixed-point equation, then rewrite the relation relative to the centre.
steps: \(z^{\prime}-\omega=-2(z-\omega)\), so this is a homothety with centre \(\Omega(1+i/3)\) and ratio \(-2\).
exercises.answer: A homothety with centre at \(1+i/3\) and ratio \(-2\). The image of \(A\) has complex coordinate \(1-i\).

quiz.explanation: Every nonzero complex number has four distinct fourth roots. The same number does not necessarily have four real roots.
