lessons.title: Number theory in ℤ
goals: Calculate a greatest common divisor and a Bézout identity.
Solve a Diophantine equation.
Use congruences and convert between number bases.
lessons.intro: Number theory studies exact relationships between integers. We ask why one number divides another and what remainder a very large power leaves, as well as calculating numerical results. We build the method from Euclidean division to congruences, identifying the assumptions that make each theorem valid.

sections.title: 1. Divisibility and Euclidean division
sections.body:
We write \(a\mid b\) if there is an integer \(k\) such that \(b=ak\). If \(a\) divides \(b\) and \(c\), it divides every integer linear combination \(ub+vc\). This is the idea used in Bézout's identity.

For every \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb N^*\), there are unique quotient and remainder values satisfying \(a=bq+r\), with \(0\leq r

sections.title: 2. Euclid's algorithm, GCD, and LCM
sections.body: The common divisors of \(a,b\) are the same as those of \(b,r\) when \(a=bq+r\). Repeat the division until the remainder is zero. The last nonzero remainder is the greatest common divisor, or GCD. For positive numbers, \(\operatorname{PGCD}(a,b)\operatorname{PPCM}(a,b)=ab\), where PGCD denotes the GCD and PPCM the least common multiple, or LCM. Distinguish a common divisor from a common multiple.

example.title: Finding the GCD and working backwards
example.statement: Calculate \(\operatorname{PGCD}(252,198)\) and express it as an integer linear combination of the two numbers.

sections.title: 3. Bézout's identity, Gauss's lemma, and Diophantine equations
sections.body:
Bézout's identity states that \(a,b\) are coprime if and only if there are \(u,v\in\mathbb Z\) with \(au+bv=1\). Gauss's lemma states that if \(a\mid bc\) and \(\operatorname{PGCD}(a,b)=1\), then \(a\mid c\). Coprimality is essential.

If \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\), the equation \(ax+by=c\) has integer solutions if and only if \(d=\operatorname{PGCD}(a,b)\) divides \(c\). Given one solution \((x_0,y_0)\), all solutions are \(x=x_0+(b/d)t\) and \(y=y_0-(a/d)t\), with \(t\in\mathbb Z\).

example.title: The complete solution family
steps: Divide by six to get \(7x+5y=1\). Notice that \(7\times3+5(-4)=1\).
Subtract the particular solution to get \(7(x-3)=-5(y+4)\). Since \(7,5\) are coprime, Gauss's lemma gives \(5\mid(x-3)\).
Write \(x=3+5t\). Substitution gives \(y=-4-7t\). Check the resulting family in the original equation.

sections.title: 4. Congruences and Fermat's little theorem
sections.body:
\(a\equiv b\pmod n\) means \(n\mid(a-b)\). We can add, multiply, and raise to a positive integer power. Division is not automatic. Cancelling a factor requires it to be invertible modulo \(n\).

If \(p\) is prime and \(p\nmid a\), Fermat's little theorem gives \(a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p\). For example, to find \(3^{100}\) modulo seven, use \(100=6\times16+4\), giving \(3^{100}\equiv3^4=81\equiv4\). Check primality and the nondivisibility condition before using the theorem.

sections.title: 5. Writing numbers in a base
sections.body:
In base \(b\geq2\), the digits run from zero to \(b-1\). The notation \((a_ka_{k-1}\ldots a_0)_b\) represents \(\sum a_jb^j\). For example, \((110101)_2=32+16+4+1=53\).

To convert from decimal to another base, repeatedly divide by the base and record the remainders, then read them from last to first. Always specify the base, because \((10)_2\) and \((10)_5\) are different numbers. Check the conversion by evaluating the sum of powers.

summary: Euclidean division gives \(a=bq+r\), with \(0\leq r<b\).
Euclid's algorithm preserves the GCD, and \(\mathrm{PGCD}\times\mathrm{PPCM}=ab\) for positive numbers.
\(ax+by=c\) has integer solutions exactly when \(\mathrm{PGCD}(a,b)\mid c\).
Gauss's lemma requires \(\mathrm{PGCD}(a,b)=1\) to infer from \(a\mid bc\) that \(a\mid c\).
Fermat's little theorem uses a prime modulus. A base representation is checked by summing powers of the base.
pitfalls: Dividing a congruence by a number without checking that it has an inverse modulo the modulus.
Giving one particular solution and forgetting the family of all integer solutions.
Reading base-conversion remainders from first to last.

exercises.title: Euclid's algorithm and the LCM
exercises.statement: Calculate the GCD and LCM of \(360\) and \(252\), then give a Bézout identity.
exercises.hint: Begin by dividing 360 by 252, then work backwards through the equalities.
steps: The last nonzero remainder is \(36\), so \(d=36\).
exercises.answer: The GCD is \(36\), the LCM is \(2520\), and \(36=-2\times360+3\times252\).

exercises.title: All integer pairs
exercises.statement: Solve \(18x+30y=12\) in \(\mathbb Z^2\).
exercises.hint: Divide the equation by \(6\), and try the solution \((-1,1)\).
steps: \(d=6\) divides \(12\), so solutions exist. The equation becomes \(3x+5y=2\).
Subtracting that solution gives \(3(x+1)=-5(y-1)\). Gauss's lemma yields \(5\mid(x+1)\).
Set \(x=-1+5t\), giving \(y=1-3t\). Substitution gives \(12\) for every \(t\in\mathbb Z\).

exercises.title: A very large power
exercises.statement: Find the remainder when \(2^{2026}\) is divided by \(7\), using Fermat's little theorem.
exercises.hint: Write \(2026=6q+r\), then reduce the smaller power.
steps: \(7\) is prime and does not divide \(2\), so \(2^6\equiv1\pmod7\).
\(16=2\times7+2\), and the remainder \(2\) lies between zero and six.

lessons.title: Algebraic structures
goals: Check the properties of a binary operation.
Recognize a group and a subgroup.
Distinguish rings, fields, and homomorphisms.
lessons.intro: In algebraic structures, naming the set is not enough. We must also identify the operation. The same set may have a different structure when the operation changes. A reliable method is to write the definition, verify every condition, and provide a clear counterexample when a condition fails.

sections.title: 1. A binary operation and its properties
sections.body:
A binary operation on \(E\) assigns to every pair of elements of \(E\) another element of \(E\). Before a lengthy calculation, check closure. For example, addition is a binary operation on \(\mathbb Z\), but division is not an operation defined on every pair with a result in the set.

Associativity compares \((a*b)*c\) with \(a*(b*c)\), while commutativity compares \(a*b\) with \(b*a\). An identity element \(e\) must satisfy both sides of \(e*a=a*e=a\). An inverse of \(a\) is an element \(a^{-1}\) satisfying \(a*a^{-1}=a^{-1}*a=e\). It is not always \(-a\) or \(1/a\). The operation determines it.

sections.title: 2. Building a proof that a structure is a group
sections.body: To show that \((G,*)\) is a group, check closure, associativity, an identity element, and an inverse for every element. If the operation is also commutative, the group is abelian. Trying two numbers can help with understanding, but it does not prove a property for every element.

example.title: An operation different from addition
example.statement: On \(G=]-1,+\infty[\), define \(x*y=x+y+xy\). Show that \((G,*)\) is an abelian group.
steps: Solving \(x*y=0\) gives \(y=-x/(1+x)\). Since \(1+y=1/(1+x)>0\), this element belongs to \(G\).
The expression is symmetric in \(x,y\), so commutativity holds.
example.answer: \((]-1,+\infty[,*)\) is an abelian group, with identity \(0\) and inverse of \(x\) equal to \(-x/(1+x)\).

sections.title: 3. Checking a subgroup
sections.body:
If \(G\) is a group and \(H\subset G\), a concise test is that \(H\) is nonempty and, for all \(x,y\in H\), \(x*y^{-1}\in H\). In an additive group, use \(x-y\). This condition combines closure, the identity, and inverses.

For example, \(3\mathbb Z\) is a subgroup of \((\mathbb Z,+)\). It contains zero, and the difference \(3m-3n=3(m-n)\) is still a multiple of three. By contrast, \(\mathbb N\) is not an additive subgroup of \(\mathbb Z\), since it contains \(1\) but not \(-1\). Closure under addition alone is insufficient.

sections.title: 4. Homomorphisms and isomorphisms
sections.body:
A homomorphism \(\varphi:(G,*)\to(H,\circ)\) preserves the operation, so \(\varphi(x*y)=\varphi(x)\circ\varphi(y)\). Specify its domain and codomain before testing this equality. An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism, allowing calculations and structure to be transferred between two groups.

For example, \(\exp:(\mathbb R,+)\to(\mathbb R_+^*,\times)\) is a homomorphism because \(e^{x+y}=e^xe^y\), and it is bijective because its inverse is \(\ln\). In contrast, the map \(x\mapsto x^2\) from \((\mathbb R,+)\) to itself is not an additive homomorphism, because \((x+y)^2\) does not always equal \(x^2+y^2\).

sections.title: 5. Rings, fields, and invertible elements
sections.body:
A ring has addition forming an abelian group, associative multiplication, and both distributive laws. Here we use the convention of a ring with identity, so a multiplicative identity \(1\) is included. A field is a commutative ring with \(1\ne0\) in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.

\(\mathbb Z\) is a ring but not a field, because \(2\) has no integer inverse. \(\mathbb Q\) is a field. In \(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z\), the class \(\overline a\) is invertible exactly when \(\operatorname{PGCD}(a,n)=1\).

example.title: Comparing two quotient rings
example.statement: Why is \(\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z\) a field, while \(\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z\) is not?
steps: Modulo five, the inverses of \(\overline1,\overline2,\overline3,\overline4\) are respectively \(\overline1,\overline3,\overline2,\overline4\).
Addition and multiplication of classes form a commutative ring, and every nonzero class has an inverse. Therefore it is a field.
Modulo six, \(\overline2\,\overline3=\overline0\), even though both factors are nonzero.
If \(\overline2\) had an inverse, multiplying this equality by it would give \(\overline3=\overline0\), a contradiction.
example.answer: \(\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z\) is a field, whereas \(\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z\) has zero divisors and is not a field.

summary: Specify the set and operation before naming the structure.
A group requires a closed binary operation, associativity, an identity, and an inverse for every element.
A subgroup is a nonempty subset closed under combining an element with the inverse of another.
A homomorphism preserves the operation. An isomorphism must also be bijective.
A field is a commutative ring with identity in which every nonzero element is invertible.
pitfalls: Confusing commutativity with associativity, which are different conditions.
Finding a formula for an inverse and forgetting to check that it belongs to the set.
Assuming every nonzero class modulo n can be divided by, even when n is composite.

exercises.title: A group with an unusual identity
exercises.statement: On \(\mathbb R\), define \(x*y=x+y-2\). Prove that this gives an abelian group.
exercises.hint: The identity must satisfy x * e = x. Solve this equation before looking for the inverse.
steps: \(x+y-2\in\mathbb R\), so the operation is closed.
\(x*y=2\) gives \(y=4-x\in\mathbb R\), the inverse for this operation.
exercises.answer: An abelian group with identity \(2\) and inverse of \(x\) equal to \(4-x\).

exercises.title: The remainder homomorphism
exercises.statement: Let \(\varphi:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z\), \(k\mapsto\overline k\). Prove that it is a surjective additive homomorphism and determine its kernel.
exercises.hint: The kernel consists of the integers whose image is the zero class.
steps: \(\varphi(a+b)=\overline{a+b}=\overline a+\overline b=\varphi(a)+\varphi(b)\), so it is a homomorphism.
Every class \(\overline r\) has a preimage \(r\), so the map is surjective.
It is not injective because \(\varphi(0)=\varphi(5)\) even though \(0\ne5\).
exercises.answer: \(\ker\varphi=5\mathbb Z\). The map is surjective and not injective.

exercises.title: Invertible elements modulo eight
exercises.statement: Determine the invertible elements of \(\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z\), and explain why this ring is not a field.
exercises.hint: Use the GCD with eight, then check the square of each odd class.
steps: The classes whose representatives have GCD with \(8\) equal to \(1\) are \(1,3,5,7\).
\(1^2\equiv3^2\equiv5^2\equiv7^2\equiv1\pmod8\), so each is its own inverse.
exercises.answer: The invertible elements are \(\overline1,\overline3,\overline5,\overline7\), and \(\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z\) is not a field.

quiz.question: For the operation x * y = x + y − 2, what is the identity element?
quiz.explanation: Solving x + e − 2 = x gives e = 2, which also satisfies the other side of the identity condition.

quiz.question: Which set is a subgroup of (ℤ,+)?
quiz.explanation: The even integers contain zero, and the difference of two even integers is even. The other two sets do not contain every additive inverse.

lessons.title: Real vector spaces
goals: Recognize a vector subspace.
Study linear independence and spanning.
Construct a basis and determine a dimension.
lessons.intro: A vector space generalizes the calculations we know for vectors. Its elements may be triples, polynomials, or even functions. What matters is that elements can be added and multiplied by real scalars while respecting the required rules. We will learn to prove that a family spans a space and understand why coordinates in a basis are unique.

sections.title: 1. The objects and the two operations
sections.body:
In a real vector space \(E\), we can add two elements and multiply an element by a scalar \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\). Addition forms an abelian group, and scalar multiplication satisfies \(\lambda(u+v)=\lambda u+\lambda v\), \((\lambda+\mu)u=\lambda u+\mu u\), \(\lambda(\mu u)=(\lambda\mu)u\), and \(1u=u\).

\(\mathbb R^2\), \(\mathbb R^3\), and the space of polynomials of degree at most two are familiar examples. The zero vector takes different forms depending on the space, such as a zero triple, the zero polynomial, or the zero function. Do not confuse a real scalar with an element of the space.

sections.title: 2. The subspace criterion
sections.body:
For \(F\subset E\) to be a subspace, it is enough to show that it is nonempty and closed under linear combinations. For all \(u,v\in F\) and \(\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R\), we require \(\lambda u+\mu v\in F\). In practice, start with the zero vector, then use the defining condition of the set.

A homogeneous linear equation often makes this check straightforward. In contrast, the plane \(x+y+z=1\) is not a subspace of \(\mathbb R^3\), because zero does not satisfy the equation. That observation alone is enough to disprove the property.

example.title: A vector plane and its basis
steps: \((0,0,0)\in F\). If \(u,v\) satisfy the equation, linearity shows that \(\lambda u+\mu v\) also satisfies it. Thus \(F\) is a subspace.
Every element of \(F\) is a combination of \(u=(2,1,0)\) and \(v=(-1,0,1)\), both of which belong to \(F\). They therefore span the space.
If \(\alpha u+\beta v=0\), the second coordinate gives \(\alpha=0\), and the third gives \(\beta=0\). The family is linearly independent.
example.answer: \((u,v)\) is a basis of \(F\), and \(\dim F=2\).

sections.title: 3. Linear combinations, spanning, and independence
sections.body:
A linear combination of \(u_1,\ldots,u_p\) is \(\lambda_1u_1+\cdots+\lambda_pu_p\). The set of all such combinations is \(\operatorname{Vect}(u_1,\ldots,u_p)\), the span. The family spans the space if every element of the space can be written this way.

To test linear independence, assume \(\lambda_1u_1+\cdots+\lambda_pu_p=0\). If the only solution has every coefficient zero, the family is linearly independent. If there is a relation with at least one nonzero coefficient, it is dependent. A family containing the zero vector is immediately dependent.

sections.title: 4. Bases, dimension, and coordinates
sections.body:
A basis is a family that is both linearly independent and spanning. Spanning guarantees existence of a representation, while independence guarantees uniqueness. The dimension is the number of elements in any basis. It need not equal the number of coordinates in the surrounding space.

In a space of dimension \(n\), a linearly independent family of \(n\) elements is a basis, as is a spanning family of \(n\) elements. A family with more than \(n\) elements is linearly dependent.

example.title: Coordinates in another basis
example.statement: Take \(u=(1,1)\) and \(v=(1,-1)\). Prove that they form a basis of \(\mathbb R^2\), and find the coordinates of \(w=(3,1)\).
steps: Two linearly independent vectors in \(\mathbb R^2\) form a basis.
example.answer: The representation is \(w=2u+v\), and its coordinates in this basis are \((2,1)\), different from its standard coordinates \((3,1)\).

sections.title: 5. A reliable method for writing proofs
sections.body:
If a space is given by equations, solve the system using parameters, then collect each parameter's coefficient to obtain spanning vectors. Do not call them a basis before checking independence. If a family is given, convert a zero linear combination into a system for the coefficients, rather than for the coordinates of an unknown vector.

The same method works with polynomials. Equality of polynomials requires equality of coefficients at each power. For example, \(a+bX+cX^2=0\) means \(a=b=c=0\), so \((1,X,X^2)\) is a basis of \(\mathbb R_2[X]\).

summary: A subspace must contain zero and be closed under linear combinations.
A linearly independent family has only the trivial zero combination, with every coefficient zero.
A spanning family gives a representation for every element of the space.
A basis combines independence and spanning, and guarantees unique coordinates.
Dimension is the number of basis elements, not the number of variables in the description.
pitfalls: Calling a spanning family a basis without checking independence.
Treating a set defined by a nonhomogeneous equation as a subspace even though it does not contain zero.
Confusing a vector's standard coordinates with its coordinates in a new basis.

exercises.title: Parametrizing a subspace
exercises.statement: Prove that \(F=\{(x,y,z):2x+y-z=0\}\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb R^3\), and determine a basis and its dimension.
exercises.hint: Express \(z\) in terms of \(x,y\).
steps: Zero satisfies the equation, and any linear combination of two solutions remains a solution because the equation is homogeneous and linear.
From the first two coordinates, \(au+bv=0\) gives \(a=b=0\), so the family is linearly independent.
exercises.answer: \((u,v)\) is a basis of \(F\), and \(\dim F=2\).

exercises.title: A dependent but useful family
exercises.statement: In \(\mathbb R^3\), take \(u=(1,0,1)\), \(v=(0,1,1)\), and \(w=(1,1,2)\). Is the family linearly independent? Determine its span and its dimension.
exercises.hint: Compare w with u + v.
steps: \(w=u+v\), so \(u+v-w=0\) is a nontrivial relation. The family is dependent.
Removing \(w\) does not change the span, since \(\operatorname{Vect}(u,v,w)=\operatorname{Vect}(u,v)\).
\(au+bv=(a,b,a+b)\), so the space is the plane \(z=x+y\).
exercises.answer: The three-vector family is dependent. Its span is \(\{(x,y,z):z=x+y\}\), with dimension \(2\).

exercises.title: Vectors that are polynomials
exercises.statement: In \(\mathbb R_2[X]\), let \(H=\{P:P(1)=0\}\). Prove that \(H\) is a subspace and find a basis.
exercises.hint: Write \(P=a+bX+cX^2\), and use \(a+b+c=0\).
steps: The zero polynomial belongs to \(H\), and \((\lambda P+\mu Q)(1)=\lambda P(1)+\mu Q(1)=0\), proving the subspace property.
The family \((X-1,X^2-1)\) spans the space. If \(\alpha(X-1)+\beta(X^2-1)=0\), the coefficient of \(X^2\) gives \(\beta=0\), and that of \(X\) gives \(\alpha=0\).

videos.description: A step-by-step visual explanation without narration. Pause at each stage to read the equation. The original video frames contain Moroccan Darija text.

quiz.question: Which test alone can be enough to disprove that a set is a subspace?
choices: It does not contain the zero vector
It is defined by an equation
quiz.explanation: Every subspace must contain zero. Its absence immediately disproves the property.

quiz.question: In a three-dimensional space, what is a linearly independent family of three elements?
choices: There is not enough information to decide
quiz.explanation: In a finite-dimensional space, a linearly independent family with as many elements as the dimension also spans the space, so it is a basis.

lessons.title: Geometry in the complex plane
goals: Calculate distances and angles using complex coordinates.
Prove collinearity or perpendicularity.
Use translations, rotations, and homotheties.
lessons.intro: We work in a plane with a positively oriented orthonormal coordinate system. The point \(M(x,y)\) has complex coordinate \(z_M=x+iy\). Complex arithmetic turns a geometric question into a short calculation. Afterwards, we interpret the result. The modulus gives a distance, the argument gives a directed angle, and a difference represents a vector.

sections.title: 1. Vectors, distances, and midpoints
sections.body:
The complex coordinate of \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) is \(z_B-z_A\), so \(AB=|z_B-z_A|\). The order of the difference matters for the vector and angle, even though reversing it does not change the distance. The midpoint of \([AB]\) has complex coordinate \((z_A+z_B)/2\).

Label the given values clearly. If \(z_A=z_B\), the points coincide and the vector \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) has no direction. This simple check prevents division by zero in a later step.

sections.title: 2. Complex quotients and angles
sections.body:
If \(A\ne B\) and \(A\ne C\), the argument of \((z_C-z_A)/(z_B-z_A)\) is the directed angle \((\overrightarrow{AB},\overrightarrow{AC})\), modulo \(2\pi\). The modulus of the quotient is \(AC/AB\).

A real quotient indicates collinearity. A nonzero purely imaginary quotient indicates perpendicularity. Both vectors must be nonzero. To prove that a triangle is isosceles, also check the modulus, not only the angle.

example.title: A right isosceles triangle
steps: The quotient equals \(i\), with modulus one and argument \(\pi/2\).
example.answer: \(AB=AC\) and \(AB\perp AC\). The triangle is right-angled and isosceles at \(A\).

sections.title: 3. Translations and rotations
sections.body:
A translation by a vector with complex coordinate \(b\) is written \(z^{\prime}=z+b\). A rotation centred at \(\Omega\), with complex coordinate \(\omega\) and angle \(\theta\), is written

\[z^{\prime}-\omega=e^{i\theta}(z-\omega).\]

Subtract the centre, multiply, then add the centre back. A rotation preserves distances. For angle \(\pi/2\), the factor is \(i\). For example, with centre \(1+i\), this rotation sends \(3+i\) to \(1+3i\).

sections.title: 4. Homotheties and fixed points
sections.body:
A homothety with centre \(\omega\) and real ratio \(k e0\) is written \(z^{\prime}-\omega=k(z-\omega)\). A negative ratio reverses direction. Distances are multiplied by \(|k|\), rather than by a negative \(k\).

For \(z^{\prime}=az+b\), with \(a e1\), the fixed point is \(\omega=b/(1-a)\). If \(|a|=1\) and \(a e1\), the transformation is a rotation. If \(a\) is real, nonzero, and different from one, it is a homothety. Find the centre by solving the fixed-point equation.

sections.title: 5. Loci defined by distances
sections.body:
\(|z-a|=R\), with \(R>0\), describes a circle centred at the point with complex coordinate \(a\) and radius \(R\). The equality \(|z-a|=|z-b|\), with \(a\ne b\), describes the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two points.

Before expanding squares, try reading the expression geometrically. For example, \(|z-2-i|=3\) is a circle with centre \((2,1)\) and radius three. If \(R=0\), the locus is a single point.

summary: \(z_{\overrightarrow{AB}}=z_B-z_A\), and \(AB=|z_B-z_A|\).
The midpoint has \(z_I=(z_A+z_B)/2\).
The quotient \((z_C-z_A)/(z_B-z_A)\) combines the directed angle and the ratio of lengths, under the required conditions.
A translation has \(z^{\prime}=z+b\). A rotation has \(z^{\prime}-\omega=e^{i\theta}(z-\omega)\).
A homothety has \(z^{\prime}-\omega=k(z-\omega)\). A circle has \(|z-a|=R\), where \(R>0\).
pitfalls: Inverting the quotient reverses the sign of the directed angle.
Check \(A\ne B\) before dividing by \(z_B-z_A\).
A rotation about a centre other than the origin requires subtracting and then restoring that centre.

exercises.title: A triangle and its circumcircle
exercises.statement: Let \(z_A=1+i\), \(z_B=3+i\), and \(z_C=1+3i\). Classify the triangle and determine the centre and radius of its circumcircle.
exercises.hint: The circumcentre of a right triangle is the midpoint of its hypotenuse.
steps: The quotient \((z_C-z_A)/(z_B-z_A)=i\) shows that the triangle is right-angled and isosceles at \(A\).
exercises.answer: The centre has complex coordinate \(2+2i\), and the radius is \(\sqrt2\).

exercises.title: Two images of the same point
exercises.statement: Let \(\omega=1+i\) and \(z_A=3+i\). Find the image of \(A\) under a rotation through \(\pi/2\), and its image under a homothety of ratio \(-2\), both with the same centre.
exercises.hint: Apply each transformation separately to A. Do not compose them.

exercises.title: Recognizing a rotation
exercises.statement: For the transformation \(z^{\prime}=iz+1-i\), determine its centre, angle, and the image of \(z_A=2+i\).
exercises.hint: Solve the fixed-point equation.
exercises.answer: The centre has complex coordinate \(1\), the angle is \(\pi/2\), and the image of \(A\) has complex coordinate \(i\).

quiz.question: If the complex quotient is \(2i\), with both vectors nonzero, what can we conclude?
quiz.explanation: The argument is \(\pi/2\), and the modulus is \(2\).

quiz.question: What does \(z^{\prime}=z+3-2i\) represent?
choices: A translation by the vector with complex coordinate \(3-2i\)
quiz.explanation: \(z^{\prime}-z\) is constant, so this is a translation.

lessons.title: Analytic geometry in three dimensions
prerequisites: The dot product in the plane
goals: Use the dot product and cross product.
Write coordinate equations for a line and a plane.
Determine intersections and calculate the distance from a point to a plane.
lessons.intro: In three-dimensional geometry, we work in an orthonormal coordinate system. A point has three coordinates, and a vector is found by subtracting the starting point's coordinates from the endpoint's. The equations have geometric meaning. A direction vector determines a line's direction, and a normal vector determines a plane's orientation.

sections.title: 1. Dot products and distances
sections.body:
If \(u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)\) and \(v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)\), then \(u\cdot v=u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3\), and \(\|u\|=\sqrt{u\cdot u}\). The distance is \(AB=\|\overrightarrow{AB}\|\).

Two nonzero vectors are perpendicular if and only if their dot product is zero. To calculate the angle, use \(\cos\theta=(u\cdot v)/(\|u\|\|v\|)\). The division requires both vectors to be nonzero.

sections.title: 2. The cross product
sections.body:
In a positively oriented coordinate system, the vector \(u\times v\) is perpendicular to \(u\) and \(v\). Its coordinates are

\[u\times v=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\ u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\ u_1v_2-u_2v_1).\]

If the cross product is zero, the vectors are linearly dependent. If it is nonzero, it provides a normal vector to the plane they span. Reversing the order reverses the sign, so \(v\times u=-u\times v\).

sections.title: 3. Lines and planes
sections.body:
The line through \(A(x_A,y_A,z_A)\) with direction vector \(u\ne0\) has parametric representation \((x,y,z)=(x_A,y_A,z_A)+tu\), with \(t\in\mathbb R\). The same parameter must appear in all three equations.

A plane with normal vector \(n=(a,b,c)\ne0\) has equation \(ax+by+cz+d=0\). To make it pass through \(A\), choose \(d=-ax_A-by_A-cz_A\). The coefficients of \(x,y,z\) give a normal vector, not a vector parallel to the plane.

example.title: A plane from a point and a normal vector
example.statement: Find the plane through \(A(1,0,2)\) perpendicular to \(n=(1,2,-1)\).

sections.title: 4. Intersecting a line and a plane
sections.body:
Substitute the line's parametric representation into the plane equation. If \(n\cdot u\ne0\), we obtain a unique value of \(t\) and therefore a unique intersection point. If \(n\cdot u=0\), the line is parallel to the plane or contained in it. Substituting a point on the line distinguishes the cases.

Two planes are parallel if their normal vectors are linearly dependent. In three dimensions, two lines may be nonparallel without intersecting, so a sketch alone is insufficient.

Two nonparallel planes intersect in a line. The cross product of their normal vectors gives a direction vector for that line. Find one point by solving both plane equations, then write a parametric representation. At each step, justify that the vector being used is nonzero.

sections.title: 5. Distance and orthogonal projection
sections.body:
The distance from \(M(x_0,y_0,z_0)\) to \(P:ax+by+cz+d=0\) is

\[d(M,P)=\frac{|ax_0+by_0+cz_0+d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}.\]

The absolute value makes the distance nonnegative. The projection of \(M\) onto the plane is \(H=M-\frac{ax_0+by_0+cz_0+d}{a^2+b^2+c^2}(a,b,c)\). Check that \(H\) belongs to the plane and \(\overrightarrow{MH}\) is parallel to \(n\). For a line \((A,u)\), the distance is \(\|\overrightarrow{AM}\times u\|/\|u\|\).

summary: \(u\cdot v=\sum_{j=1}^{3}u_jv_j\). A zero dot product establishes perpendicularity.
\(u\times v\) is perpendicular to both vectors and vanishes when they are linearly dependent.
A line has \(M=A+tu\), with \(u\ne0\) and the same \(t\) in all three coordinates.
A plane has \(ax+by+cz+d=0\), with normal vector \((a,b,c)\ne(0,0,0)\).
pitfalls: A dot product is a number and a cross product is a vector. They are different operations.
Two nonparallel lines in space do not necessarily intersect.
Remember the absolute value in the distance formula and the nonzero conditions for vectors.

exercises.title: Distance and projection
exercises.statement: Let \(P:x+2y+2z-6=0\) and \(M(1,1,1)\). Calculate the distance and the orthogonal projection.
exercises.hint: The normal vector is \((1,2,2)\), and its squared norm is nine.

exercises.title: Intersecting a line and a plane
exercises.statement: Let \(D:(x,y,z)=(t,t,1)\) and \(P:x+y+z-3=0\). Determine the intersection.
exercises.hint: Substitute all three coordinates into the plane equation.
steps: Substitute the same value into the representation to get \((x,y,z)=(1,1,1)\).

exercises.title: A plane through three points
exercises.statement: Let \(A(1,0,0)\), \(B(0,1,0)\), and \(C(0,0,1)\). Find an equation of \((ABC)\), then the distance from \(M(1,1,1)\) to it.
exercises.hint: Use the cross product to find a normal vector.
steps: \(\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=(1,1,1)\ne0\), so the points are not collinear.

videos.description: A step-by-step visual explanation without narration. Pause at each stage to read the equation. The original video frames contain Moroccan Darija text.

quiz.question: Which vector is normal to \(2x-y+3z+7=0\)?
quiz.explanation: Read the coefficients of x, y, and z.

quiz.question: If \(n\cdot u=0\), is the line always contained in the plane?
choices: No, a point on the line must be checked
quiz.explanation: The line may be parallel and outside the plane. Whether one point belongs to the plane determines the case.

lessons.title: Spheres, planes, and lines
prerequisites: Completing the square and quadratic equations
goals: Extract a sphere's centre and radius from its equation.
Determine a plane's position relative to a sphere and prove the intersection-radius formula.
Calculate the intersection of a sphere and a line, and write a tangent plane equation.
lessons.intro: We work in an orthonormal coordinate system. Here, a sphere means the surface consisting of points at the same distance from the centre. The interior together with the surface forms a closed ball. The distinction matters because the sphere's equation uses equality, whereas an interior point has distance less than the radius.

sections.title: 1. Deriving the equation from distance
sections.body:
A sphere with centre \(\Omega(a,b,c)\) and radius \(R>0\) consists of points \(M(x,y,z)\) satisfying \(\Omega M=R\). Squaring the distance gives

\[(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2+(z-c)^2=R^2.\]

When reading the centre, pay attention to the signs inside the parentheses. For example, \((y+2)^2=(y-(-2))^2\), so the centre's coordinate is \(-2\), not \(2\).

sections.title: 2. Completing the square to find the centre
sections.body:
For an equation of the form \(x^2+y^2+z^2-2ax-2by-2cz+d=0\), complete each square. The candidate centre is \((a,b,c)\), and the squared radius is \(R^2=a^2+b^2+c^2-d\).

If this quantity is positive, the locus is a sphere. If it is zero, the locus is a single point. If it is negative, there are no real points. Check the sign before writing a radius.

example.title: The centre and the correct signs

sections.title: 3. Intersecting a sphere and a plane, with proof
sections.body:
Calculate \(d=d(\Omega,P)\), and let \(H\) be the centre's projection onto the plane. If \(d>R\), the intersection is empty. If \(d=R\), the plane is tangent at \(H\). If \(d

For the proof, take any \(M\in P\). The triangle \(\Omega HM\) is right-angled at \(H\), so \(\Omega M^2=d^2+HM^2\). For \(M\) to lie on the sphere, we need \(HM^2=R^2-d^2\). The sign of the right-hand side explains the three cases.

example.title: A circle of intersection
example.statement: A sphere is centred at the origin with radius \(5\). The plane is \(z=3\).
example.answer: A circle with centre \((0,0,3)\) and radius \(4\).

sections.title: 4. Intersecting a sphere and a line
sections.body:
Substitute the representation \(M=A+tu\), with \(u\ne0\), into the sphere equation. The result is a quadratic polynomial with leading coefficient \(\|u\|^2>0\),

\[\|u\|^2t^2+2u\cdot\overrightarrow{\Omega A}\,t+\Omega A^2-R^2=0.\]

If the discriminant is positive, there are two intersection points. If it is zero, there is one point of tangency. If it is negative, the line does not meet the sphere. Substitute each value of \(t\) back into all three coordinates.

sections.title: 5. The tangent plane
sections.body:
If \(A\) lies on the sphere, the tangent plane at \(A\) is perpendicular to the radius vector \(\overrightarrow{\Omega A}\), with equation

\[\overrightarrow{AM}\cdot\overrightarrow{\Omega A}=0.\]

To prove this, every point \(M\) in the plane satisfies \(\Omega M^2=R^2+AM^2\). The equality \(\Omega M=R\) occurs only if \(M=A\), so the intersection contains just one point. First check that \(A\) really lies on the sphere.

summary: \(R^2>0\) gives a sphere, \(R^2=0\) a point, and \(R^2<0\) an empty set.
A plane at distance \(d\) from the centre is outside if \(d>R\), tangent if \(d=R\), and cuts the sphere if \(d<R\).
The intersection circle is centred at the projection of the sphere's centre and has radius \(\sqrt{R^2-d^2}\).
The tangent plane at \(A\) has normal vector \(\overrightarrow{\Omega A}\). Find a line intersection by substitution.
pitfalls: The centre's coordinates use the opposite signs to the constants inside the parentheses.
The intersection circle's radius is usually smaller than the sphere's radius.
For a line, a parameter solution is not yet a point. Substitute it into the coordinates.

exercises.title: Centre, radius, and tangent plane
exercises.statement: Let \(S:x^2+y^2+z^2-2x+4y-6z+5=0\). Determine the centre, radius, and tangent plane at \(A(4,-2,3)\).
exercises.hint: Complete the squares, then calculate the radius vector.
steps: \(\overrightarrow{\Omega A}=(3,0,0)\) is normal to the tangent plane.
exercises.answer: The centre is \((1,-2,3)\), the radius is \(3\), and the tangent plane is \(x=4\).

exercises.title: Three positions of a plane
exercises.statement: Let \(S:x^2+y^2+z^2=25\). Determine its intersection with \(z=3\), then \(z=5\), then \(z=6\).
exercises.hint: Compare each plane's distance from the origin with five.
steps: For \(z=3\), the distance is three, giving a circle with centre \((0,0,3)\) and radius \(\sqrt{25-9}=4\).
For \(z=5\), the distance is five, giving the point of tangency \((0,0,5)\).
For \(z=6\), the distance exceeds the radius, so there is no intersection.
exercises.answer: A circle, then one point, then the empty set, respectively.

exercises.statement: Let \(S:x^2+y^2+z^2=9\) and \(D:(x,y,z)=(t,1,2)\). Find the intersection points.
exercises.hint: Substitute before calculating a discriminant.
steps: Return to the parametric representation for each value.

lessons.title: Counting methods
goals: Distinguish ordered arrangements from unordered selections.
Determine whether repetition or replacement is allowed.
Use arrangements and combinations without double counting.
lessons.intro: Before using a formula, answer two questions. Does order matter? Can the same item be used again? Choosing a committee differs from awarding the top places in a competition. Reordering the same people leaves a committee unchanged, but changes a podium result. This distinction determines the counting method.

sections.title: 1. The addition and multiplication principles
sections.body:
If a choice is made in stages, multiply the number of possibilities at each stage, accounting for what has changed after previous selections. Four shirts and three pairs of trousers give \(4\times3=12\) outfits.

If the cases are split into disjoint categories, add their counts. To use addition, ensure that the same case is not counted in two categories. Sometimes the easiest method is to count everything and subtract the forbidden cases.

sections.title: 2. Ordered selections with repetition
sections.body:
Suppose there are \(n\) items and we want to fill \(p\) ordered positions, allowing repetition. Each position still has \(n\) choices, so the count is \(n^p\). This model fits, for example, a code whose digits may repeat.

The formula does not apply automatically when the first position has a special restriction. In a four-digit number, zero cannot occupy the first position. Handle this position separately before multiplying.

example.title: A code with repetition
example.statement: A code has three positions, uses five different symbols, and allows repetition.
steps: The first position has five choices, as do the second and third.
Order matters. The code ABC differs from BAC.

sections.title: 3. Ordered selections without repetition
sections.body:
To select \(p\) ordered items from \(n\) distinct items without repetition, with \(0\le p\le n\), the number of possibilities is

\[A_n^p=n(n-1)\cdots(n-p+1)=\frac{n!}{(n-p)!}.\]

There is one fewer choice each time because a used item is not returned. If every item is arranged, \(p=n\), giving \(n!\), the number of permutations of distinct items. By convention, \(0!=1\).

example.title: A winners' podium
example.statement: Award three distinct places among five competitors, with no ties.
steps: There are five choices for first place, four for second, and three for third.
The same three competitors in a different order count as another result.

sections.title: 4. Unordered selections and combinations
sections.body:
A committee of \(p\) people chosen from \(n\), without repetition or distinct roles, is counted by

\[\binom np=\frac{n!}{p!(n-p)!}.\]

Why divide by \(p!\)? An ordered arrangement counts the same group in every possible order. Three committee members can be arranged in six ways, but they still form one committee. Also, \(\binom np=\binom n{n-p}\), because choosing the members is equivalent to choosing who is left out.

sections.title: 5. Combined conditions and checking the result
sections.body:
When there are categories, identify how many items are required from each, then multiply the independent selection counts. A committee containing two girls from four and one boy from three is counted by \(\binom42\binom31\).

The phrase “at least” often suggests using the complement. To choose a committee of three from seven people, comprising four girls and three boys, with at least one girl, count all \(\binom73\) committees and subtract the single all-boy committee. Check that the resulting integer is nonnegative and no greater than the total number of cases.

summary: Multiply for successive stages. Add disjoint cases without double counting.
Ordered selections with repetition give \(n^p\) when the same choices are available in every position.
Ordered selections without repetition give \(A_n^p=n!/(n-p)!\). Arranging \(n\) distinct items gives \(n!\).
Unordered selections without repetition give \(\binom np=n!/[p!(n-p)!]\).
For “at least,” try the total minus the complement. Clarify the conditions before choosing a formula.
pitfalls: A committee has no ordering unless members are assigned different roles.
Sampling with replacement does not reduce the number of items available for the next draw.
A multidigit number cannot start with zero. A secret code may allow it if the statement says so.

exercises.title: Four-digit numbers
exercises.statement: How many four-digit numbers with distinct digits can be formed using digits zero through nine? How many are possible if repetition is allowed?
exercises.hint: There are nine choices for the first digit. Zero can appear in the second position.
steps: Without repetition, the first digit has \(9\) choices and the second also has \(9\), because one digit has been used but zero is now allowed.
The third has \(8\) choices and the fourth \(7\), giving \(9\times9\times8\times7=4536\).

exercises.title: A committee with a condition
exercises.statement: There are four girls and three boys. Count committees of three, first with two girls and one boy, then with at least one girl.
exercises.hint: For the second question, subtract the all-boy committee from the total.
steps: Two girls and one boy gives \(\binom42\binom31=6\times3=18\).
A committee with no girls gives \(\binom33=1\), so \(35-1=34\).
exercises.answer: There are \(18\) committees under the first condition and \(34\) under the second.

exercises.title: Drawing simultaneously
exercises.statement: A bag contains five red balls and three blue balls, each distinguished by a number. Draw three at once. Count all possible draws, then those containing two red balls and one blue ball.
exercises.hint: The draw is simultaneous, so order does not matter.
steps: Choose two red balls from five in \(\binom52=10\) ways.
Choose one blue ball from three in \(\binom31=3\) ways. Multiply to obtain \(10\times3=30\).
exercises.answer: The total is \(56\), and the required draws number \(30\).

quiz.explanation: The roles are different and repetition is not allowed, so \(A_5^2=5\times4=20\).

quiz.explanation: The same group remains the same committee. Use combinations rather than ordered arrangements.

lessons.title: Probability and conditional probability
goals: Describe events and use unions, intersections, and complements.
Distinguish independence from mutual exclusivity.
Calculate conditional probabilities using total probability and Bayes' theorem.
lessons.intro: Before calculating, specify the experiment, its possible outcomes, and the event of interest. Conditional probability introduces information that changes the set of cases we consider. This explains the difference between the initial probability of drawing a red ball and the probability after learning the colour of the first ball.

sections.title: 1. Events and basic rules
sections.body:
The sample space is \(\Omega\), and an event \(A\) is a subset of it. We have \(0\le P(A)\le1\), \(P(\Omega)=1\), and \(P(\overline A)=1-P(A)\). Only when elementary outcomes are equally likely may we use \(P(A)=|A|/|\Omega|\).

The union \(A\cup B\) means at least one event occurs, while the intersection \(A\cap B\) means both occur. The general formula is \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\). Subtract the intersection because it has been counted twice.

sections.title: 2. Conditional probability
sections.body:
Given the information that \(B\) has occurred, with \(P(B)>0\), the conditional probability is

\[P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.\]

It can also be written \(P_B(A)\). The order of the events matters. \(P(A\mid B)\) is not always \(P(B\mid A)\). Rearranging the formula gives \(P(A\cap B)=P(B)P(A\mid B)\). In a probability tree, multiply the branch probabilities along the same path.

example.title: Two draws without replacement
example.statement: A bag contains three red balls and two blue balls. Draw two successively without replacement. Calculate the probability that both are red.
steps: After drawing a red ball, two red balls remain among four, so \(P(R_2\mid R_1)=2/4\).

sections.title: 3. Independence and mutual exclusivity
sections.body:
Events are independent if \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\). If \(P(B)>0\), this is equivalent to \(P(A\mid B)=P(A)\). Knowing that \(B\) occurred does not change the probability of \(A\).

Mutual exclusivity means \(A\cap B=\varnothing\), so the events cannot occur together. Two mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are not independent, because the intersection has probability zero while the product of their probabilities is positive. Distinguish these properties using their definitions.

sections.title: 4. The law of total probability
sections.body:
If \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\) partition \(\Omega\) into disjoint and exhaustive cases, each with \(P(A_j)>0\), then

\[P(B)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}P(A_j)P(B\mid A_j).\]

Add the probabilities of the different paths leading to the same event. In a tree with two sources, each path needs the source's probability and the event's conditional probability within that source. Do not add conditional probabilities alone without their weights.

example.title: An exercise with two machines
example.statement: Machine \(M_1\) produces \(60\%\) of the output and \(M_2\) produces \(40\%\). Their stated defect rates are \(2\%\) and \(5\%\).

sections.title: 5. Bayes' theorem, from an outcome back to its source
sections.body:
When a part is known to be defective and we want the probability of its source, use

\[P(A_j\mid B)=\frac{P(A_j)P(B\mid A_j)}{P(B)},\qquad P(B)>0.\]

In the machine example, the probability that a defective part came from \(M_2\) is \(0.02/0.032=5/8\). This differs from the machine's production share because the new information is that the part is defective. The question is reversed through conditional probability, not by arbitrarily inverting a fraction.

summary: \(P(\overline A)=1-P(A)\), and \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\).
\(P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)\), provided \(P(B)>0\).
Independence means \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\). Mutual exclusivity means an empty intersection.
For total probability, sum \(P(A_j)P(B\mid A_j)\) over a disjoint and exhaustive partition.
Bayes' theorem gives \(P(A_j\mid B)=P(A_j)P(B\mid A_j)/P(B)\).
pitfalls: Swapping the event and the condition changes the question and usually the answer.
Without replacement, the bag's contents change. Do not directly reuse the first-draw probability for the second draw.
Favourable outcomes divided by all outcomes is valid only when elementary outcomes are equally likely.

exercises.title: Events for a fair die
exercises.statement: Roll a fair die. Let \(A\) be the event that the number is even and \(B\) the event that it is greater than four. Calculate \(P(A\cup B)\) and check independence.
exercises.hint: Write the sets before calculating.
exercises.answer: The union has probability \(2/3\), and the events are independent.

exercises.title: The probability on the second draw
exercises.statement: There are three red balls and two blue balls, with two draws without replacement. Calculate \(P(R_1\cap R_2)\) and \(P(R_2)\), then check independence.
exercises.hint: For red on the second draw, split according to the first ball's colour.
exercises.answer: \(P(R_1\cap R_2)=3/10\), and \(P(R_2)=3/5\). The events are not independent.

exercises.title: From a defect back to the machine
exercises.hint: Start with total probability, then use Bayes' theorem.
steps: The two machines form a partition, so \(P(D)=0.6(0.02)+0.4(0.05)=0.032\).
exercises.answer: The defect probability is \(3.2\%\). The probability that a defective part came from \(M_2\) is \(62.5\%\).

lessons.title: Random variables and the binomial distribution
lessons.titleAr: Random variables and the binomial distribution
goals: Construct the probability distribution of a finite random variable.
Calculate expectation, variance, and standard deviation.
Recognize the conditions for a binomial distribution and apply it.
lessons.intro: A random variable \(X\) assigns a real number to each experimental outcome, such as the number of red balls, the number of successes, or a value specified in an exercise. To study \(X\), we need its possible values and the probability of each value. Its expected value need not be an outcome possible in a single experiment.

sections.title: 1. Constructing a probability distribution
sections.body:
If the values of \(X\) are \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\), calculate \(p_j=P(X=x_j)\). Present the distribution in a table. Every probability must lie between zero and one, and the sum must be one,

\[p_j\ge0,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^{m}p_j=1.\]

Partition the outcomes by the value of \(X\), without duplication or omission. If the probabilities do not add to one, check the table before calculating expectation and variance. For sampling without replacement, counting methods provide the appropriate distribution.

sections.title: 2. Expected value
sections.body:
The expected value is the average weighted by the probabilities,

\[E(X)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_jp_j.\]

Values with greater probabilities have more influence. Expectation gives a theoretical centre of the distribution, without guaranteeing the result of each experiment. A fair die has expected value \(3.5\), even though no face shows three and a half.

If \(Y=aX+b\), linearity gives \(E(Y)=aE(X)+b\). No independence assumption is needed to apply this property to the same random variable.

sections.title: 3. Variance and standard deviation
sections.body:
Variance measures spread around the expected value. Two equivalent formulas are

\[V(X)=\sum_j(x_j-E(X))^2p_j=E(X^2)-E(X)^2.\]

Calculate \(E(X^2)=\sum_jx_j^2p_j\), then subtract the square of the expected value, not the expected value itself. Variance is nonnegative, and the standard deviation is \(\sigma(X)=\sqrt{V(X)}\). Adding a constant does not change the spread, and \(V(aX+b)=a^2V(X)\).

sections.title: 4. Conditions for a binomial distribution
sections.body:
Repeat \(n\) independent trials, each with success or failure and a constant success probability \(p\). If \(X\) counts successes, write \(X\sim\mathcal B(n,p)\). Having two outcomes alone is insufficient. Independence and a constant probability are also required.

For \(0\[P(X=k)=\binom nkp^k(1-p)^{n-k}.\]

Choose the positions of the successes in \(\binom nk\) ways, and each specific arrangement has probability \(p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\). If \(p=0\), then \(X=0\) always. If \(p=1\), then \(X=n\) always.

sections.title: 5. Binomial expectation, variance, and complements
sections.body:
If \(X\sim\mathcal B(n,p)\), then \(E(X)=np\) and \(V(X)=np(1-p)\). For the probability of at least one success, the complement is often easier,

\[P(X\ge1)=1-P(X=0)=1-(1-p)^n.\]

For example, in four independent tosses of a fair coin, the number of heads follows \(\mathcal B(4,1/2)\), with expected value two. This does not mean that every sequence must contain exactly two heads.

summary: A probability distribution gives values \(x_j\) and probabilities \(p_j\ge0\), with \(\sum p_j=1\).
\(E(X)=\sum x_jp_j\), and \(E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b\).
\(V(X)=E(X^2)-E(X)^2\), \(\sigma=\sqrt V\), and \(V(aX+b)=a^2V(X)\).
A binomial distribution requires \(n\) independent trials with the same success probability, and \(X\) must count successes.
For \(X\sim\mathcal B(n,p)\), \(P(X=k)=\binom nkp^k(1-p)^{n-k}\), \(E=np\), and \(V=np(1-p)\).
pitfalls: Expectation is not a guaranteed result for each experiment and may not be a possible value.
For variance, subtract the square of the expected value. A negative result signals a calculation error.
Sampling without replacement generally does not produce independence, so do not immediately assume a binomial distribution.

exercises.title: A distribution with negative and positive values
exercises.statement: \(X\) takes values \(-1,0,2\) with probabilities \(1/4,1/2,1/4\). Calculate expectation, variance, and standard deviation.
exercises.hint: Calculate \(E(X^2)\) as a separate step.

exercises.title: Four independent tosses
exercises.statement: Toss a fair coin independently four times. Let \(X\) be the number of heads. Calculate \(P(X=2)\), \(P(X\ge1)\), the expectation, and the variance.
exercises.hint: Check the binomial conditions, then use the complement for the second question.
steps: \(X\sim\mathcal B(4,1/2)\), because the tosses are independent and the probability is constant.

exercises.title: A distribution from sampling without replacement
exercises.statement: A bag contains three white balls and two black balls, all distinguishable and equally likely to be selected. Draw two at once. Let \(X\) count the white balls. Find the distribution, then its expectation and variance.
exercises.hint: There are \(\binom52=10\) possible draws, and X can be zero, one, or two.
exercises.answer: The distribution is \((0,1/10),(1,6/10),(2,3/10)\), with \(E=6/5\) and \(V=9/25\). It is not binomial because sampling is without replacement.
